text: Before you start Turn the benchtop shaker to 37 °C (or use an incubator). Prepare PBSTB (PBS + 0.01% BSA + 0.05% Tween 80) and chill it on ice. Thaw 2% PFA in PBS. Optional: 1 mg/mL glycine in PBS. Grow a secondary culture overnight to log phase and record the OD₆₀₀. Probe pulse (200 µL culture per condition) Probe Stock Final Add per 200 µL no probe none none none alkDD 500 mM 2.5 mM 1 µL Oalk-TMM 2.5 mM 50 µM 4 µL alkD-Ala 50 mM 500 µM 2 µL Rotate at 37 °C for 10 min. Spin 3,500 × g, 5 min. Wash 3× with cold PBSTB (spin 3,500 × g, 5 min each). Fix with 2% formaldehyde, 10 min at room temperature with rotation/shaking. Wash 3× with PBSTB. Optional: quench in 1 mg/mL glycine in PBS for 15 min at room temperature, then wash 3× with room-temperature PBSTB. Click reaction (master mix for 4 samples, in 900 µL PBSTB) Add the reagents in this order, mixing between additions: Reagent Stock Final µL per reaction mix CuSO₄ 50 mM 1 mM 20 TBTA 6.4 mM 128 µM 20 Sodium ascorbate (fresh) 60 mM (11.9 mg/mL in water) 1 mM 20 Azide fluorophore (e.g. picolyl azide AF488; or AF647, TAMRA, CR110) 1 mM 40 µM 40 Resuspend each sample in 200 µL click master mix. Incubate 30 min – 1 h at room temperature with shaking/rotation. Wash 3× with PBSTB. Protect from light and store at 4 °C. TBTA and picolyl-azide dyes are available from Click Chemistry Tools; sodium ascorbate from Sigma (A7631). Green picolyl azide 488 is the usual choice; TAMRA also works when green is not available. Include a no-probe control and a no-dye control. Check that the picolyl azide quantity (40 µL of 1 mM into ~1 mL, 40 µM) matches the total volume used.

Purpose Make LB agar plates, with or without antibiotic, for E. coli work. A working-concentration table for E. coli and mycobacteria is included. Media LB broth: dissolve 20 g LB broth powder per 1 L water, then autoclave. LB comes in several formulations: low salt (Lennox or Luria) and high salt (Miller). Use low-salt LB for hygromycin and zeocin. They do not work well in high-salt (Miller) LB. LB agar (500 mL): 7.5 g LB agar powder + 10 g LB broth powder, brought to 500 mL with RO water in a 1L autoclave bottle. Do not overfill. Autoclave. Pouring plates Heat the LB agar until it is completely dissolved. Without antibiotic: pour into sterile Petri dishes to about halfway. With antibiotic: let the molten agar cool until the bottle is comfortable to hold for about 10 seconds with your bare hand. Antibiotic added to agar that is too hot will be degraded. Add the antibiotic, mix by swirling, then pour into sterile Petri dishes. Immediately after pouring, pass a flame (a fire torch works) quickly over the surface to pop bubbles. Let plates set and cool on the bench, lids closed, for about 16-24h, then store. Do not leave out longer than 24h or without lids on, as they may dry out or become contaminated. Working concentrations Antibiotic E. coli Mycobacteria Notes Kanamycin 50 µg/mL 25 µg/mL Hygromycin B 100–150 µg/mL 50 µg/mL Use low-salt LB for E. coli. Zeocin 25 µg/mL 20 µg/mL Use low-salt LB for E. coli. Apramycin 30 µg/mL 30 µg/mL Apramycin resistance protects against kanamycin, but not the reverse. Ampicillin 100 µg/mL or 140 µg/mL depending on the protocol not used Store plates no more than ~1 month at 4 °C. Carbenicillin 100 µg/mL not used More stable than ampicillin. Tetracycline 10 µg/mL not used Dissolve in ethanol, store at −20 °C. Chloramphenicol 25 µg/mL not used Dissolve in ethanol, store at 4 °C. Gentamicin 15 µg/mL 5 µg/mL Nourseothricin 40 µg/mL 20 µg/mL Streptomycin 50 µg/mL 20 µg/mL Anhydrotetracycline (inducer) n/a 25–500 ng/mL See induction systems. Rifampicin, isoniazid, trimethoprim, streptomycin, ethionamide, ethambutol, ciprofloxacin and amikacin are used for killing or susceptibility testing of mycobacteria, not for selection. MICs vary between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis. Where it usually fails Antibiotic does not seem to work. The agar was probably too hot when it went in, or hygromycin/zeocin was used in high-salt LB. Satellite colonies on ampicillin plates. They appear when plates are incubated longer than about 16–18 hours at 37 °C. Carbenicillin is more stable and reduces the problem. Bubbles in plates. Flame the surface right after pouring.

Purpose Move a plasmid from a diaminopimelic acid (DAP) auxotroph E. coli donor into a recipient strain by mating cells on solid medium, then select recipients that received the plasmid. Because the donor cannot grow without DAP, plating the mating mixture on medium lacking DAP counter-selects the donor. Before you start Donor: E. coli DAP auxotroph carrying the plasmid to be transferred (kanamycin-marked in this example). Grow with DAP. Recipient: the strain that will receive the plasmid. Grow without antibiotic. Media and reagents: YG broth and agar, LB broth, DAP stock (60 mM), kanamycin, 1X PBS. Plates: YG + DAP (mating plates) and YG + kanamycin 30 µg/mL (selection plates). Set up every donor × recipient combination you want. This example uses 2 donors × 2 recipients = 4 combinations. Day 1: overnight cultures Recipient: 10 mL YG broth, no antibiotic, in a 125 mL flask. Shake at 225 rpm, 28 °C. Donor: 10 mL LB + kanamycin 50 µg/mL + DAP (50 µL of 60 mM stock, about 0.3 mM final). Grow in a roller drum at 37 °C. Day 2: mating In the afternoon, transfer 1 mL of each overnight culture to a separate microcentrifuge tube. Wash each pellet twice with 1X PBS: spin 3000 rpm for 5 min, resuspend in 500 µL PBS each time. After the second wash, resuspend in 500 µL 1X PBS. In new tubes, combine donor and recipient to a total of 100 µL. Mix by pipetting, not vortexing. Volumes used: 50 µL donor + 50 µL recipient (1:1) 10 µL donor + 90 µL recipient (a 1:9 donor:recipient ratio by volume) 1 µL donor + 99 µL recipient (a 1:99 donor:recipient ratio by volume) Spot the entire 100 µL onto a YG + DAP plate. Do not spread. Use one plate per donor × recipient combination, with the three ratios spotted on the same plate. Let the spots dry, then incubate at 28 °C overnight. Day 3 onward: recover transconjugants Check for growth in the spots the next morning. If none, check again later that day, then the following morning. When growth appears, scrape the spot and suspend in 1 mL 1X PBS. Spin and wash twice more in 1 mL PBS (same spin as above). Resuspend the final pellet in 100 µL PBS and spread the entire volume on a YG + kanamycin 30 µg/mL plate (no DAP). Incubate overnight at 28 °C. When colonies appear, screen by colony PCR with primers specific to the transferred plasmid. See the colony PCR protocol. If you see a lawn rather than single colonies, take a small amount and streak for single colonies first, then screen. Pick 3 single colonies per donor × recipient combination, grow in YG + kanamycin 30 µg/mL, and make freezer stocks. Where it usually fails No growth in the mating spot. Check again later the same day, then the next morning. Confirm DAP was in the mating plates. A lawn on the selection plate. Streak out for single colonies before colony PCR, so you do not screen a mixed population. Donor carry-over. If donor growth appears on selection plates, confirm they contain no DAP and that the post-mating washes were done twice.

Stock dilutions TAE: dilute a 50X stock for running and pouring agarose gels. PBS: dilute a 10X stock. Tris-glycine-SDS: running buffer for tris-glycine gels; dilute from 10X. Tris-glycine transfer buffer (SDS-PAGE): dilute from 10X and add 10–20% methanol. 6X sample loading buffer Component Final in 6X Tris-Cl pH 6.8 300 mM SDS 12% (w/v) Bromophenol blue 0.6% (w/v) Glycerol 60% DTT 600 mM 6X Laemmli buffer (50 mL) Combine 15 mL 1 M Tris-Cl pH 6.8, 6 g SDS, 0.3 g bromophenol blue and 30 mL 100% glycerol. When fully dissolved, cool on ice or in the fridge. Add 4.63 g DTT (FW 154.24) and stir quickly, keeping the solution on ice.

Medium Ingredient 1 L 500 mL 250 mL KH₂PO₄ 0.5 g 0.25 g 0.125 g MgSO₄·7H₂O 0.5 g 0.25 g 0.125 g Citric acid (see note 1) 2.0 g 1.0 g 0.5 g Ferric ammonium citrate 0.05 g 0.025 g 0.0125 g (NH₄)₂SO₄ (see note 2) 0.5 g 0.25 g 0.125 g ZnSO₄, 1% solution 0.1 mL 0.05 mL 0.025 mL Carbon source, 20% solution (see note 3) 10–40 mL 5–20 mL 2.5–10 mL Tyloxapol, 10% solution 5 mL 2.5 mL 1.25 mL ddH₂O to 1000 mL to 500 mL to 250 mL Dissolve the salts in warm distilled water, about one-third of the final volume. Add the carbon source and tyloxapol, and bring to volume with ddH₂O. Adjust the pH to about 7.4, then filter sterilize. Optionally, make the Sauton’s base without carbon source and add filter-sterilized carbon source as desired. Notes Previous experiments suggest that M. tuberculosis cannot use citric acid as a carbon source. Ammonium sulfate replaces asparagine, because M. tuberculosis can use asparagine as a carbon source. The 0.5 g/L concentration is based on 7H9 medium. The optimal final carbon-source concentration depends on the experiment. For a single carbon source use 0.2–0.4% glucose or glycerol (0.4% glucose gives more robust growth than 0.2%), or 0.2% acetate or fatty acids. Propionate and valerate may need to be reduced to 0.1%, since toxicity is sometimes seen at 0.2%. When combining two carbon sources, use 0.1% of each. 20% carbon-source stocks (filter sterilize) Stock Preparation Glucose 1 g, brought to 5 mL with ddH₂O Acetate 1 g sodium acetate (C₂H₃NaO₂), brought to 5 mL with ddH₂O Glycerol 1 mL, brought to 5 mL with ddH₂O Propionic acid 1 mL, brought to 5 mL with ddH₂O Butyric acid 1 mL, brought to 5 mL with ddH₂O. It smells strongly: prepare in a chemical hood and dispose of waste in a closed container. Valeric acid (C₅H₁₀O₂) 1 mL, brought to 5 mL with 50% ethanol Hexanoic acid (C₆H₁₂O₂) 1 mL, brought to 5 mL with 50% ethanol The ethanol carried over with the fatty acids is small relative to the fatty acid, and slow-growing mycobacteria seem unable to metabolize ethanol (Pandey and Sassetti, PNAS 2008; Tsukamura, Tubercle 1988). The source notes a final ethanol concentration of 0.02% for 0.1% fatty acid; by my calculation it is closer to 0.2%. Please check.

Purpose Screen colonies for an insert, plasmid or integration using a Taq-based master mix. Taq has low fidelity, so use this for checking only, never for cloning. Reaction (10 µL) For a Taq master mix that is supplied as a 2X mix with salts, dNTPs and loading dye (for example GoTaq): Component Volume 2X Taq master mix 5 µL Forward primer, 10 µM 0.5 µL Reverse primer, 10 µM 0.5 µL DMSO 0.5 µL Water 3.5 µL, minus the volume of template added Make a master mix for the number of colonies plus 2 to allow for pipetting error, and aliquot 10 µL per PCR tube. Number the tubes. E. coli Use a sterile tip to pick a colony. Patch the colony onto a numbered spot on a plate with the correct antibiotic, then put the same tip into the PCR tube with the matching number. Run the colony PCR program on the thermocycler. Mycobacteria Pick a colony onto a plate to keep it, then transfer some into 10 µL water. Do not boil. Use 1 µL of this per reaction. An older approach is to suspend the colony in 10 µL DMSO and heat in a thermocycler for an hour to lyse the cells. This can release too much DNA and inhibit the reaction, so water without boiling is preferred. Add 1 µL of lysate to the reaction and run as for E. coli. Where it usually fails No band from mycobacterial colonies, but a positive control works. Try a few colonies with a high-fidelity polymerase (Phusion) with a 5–10 min initial step at 98 °C to lyse cells. Lysate seems to inhibit the reaction. DMSO-boiled lysates can carry over too much DNA. Switch to a water suspension without boiling. Mixed or lawn growth. Re-streak to single colonies before screening.

What they are E. coli with the plasmid-copy-number gene pcnB under an inducible promoter. ColE1/pMB1-origin plasmids (pUC, pET types) are kept at low copy number (about 9 copies for pUC19, versus ~216 in the parent strain) until the CopyCutter Induction Solution is added, which raises copy number (pUC19 ~200 copies). Genotype: mcrA Δ(mrr-hsdRMS-mcrBC) recA1 endA1 ΔpcnB, T1-phage resistant, blue/white compatible. Cautions Plasmids are distributed randomly to daughter cells at low copy; 10–60% of cells can lack plasmid. Kanamycin selection gives fewer plasmid-free cells than ampicillin. Not recommended for vectors that need tetracycline selection. Store cells at –70 °C; do not refreeze chemically competent cells. Electroporation DNA in water or low-salt buffer (e.g. TE). Prepare 1 mL antibiotic-free LB per sample; pre-chill cuvettes. Thaw 50 µL cells on ice; mix gently with DNA (avoid bubbles); electroporate with your E. coli settings. Immediately add 950 µL room-temperature LB, move to a 15 mL tube, shake at 37 °C, 220–230 rpm for 1 h. Plate on LB with antibiotic. Control: 10 pg pUC19 (dilute the supplied 100 pg/µL DNA 1:10 and use 1 µL); plate on ampicillin 100 µg/mL. Chemical transformation Standard (highest efficiency): thaw on ice; add 1–5 µL DNA/ligation; ice 5–30 min; 42 °C for 30 s; ice 2 min; add 250 µL SOC; 37 °C for 60 min with shaking (225 rpm); plate. Five-minute procedure (ampicillin only; ≥10-fold lower efficiency): add 3–5 µL DNA, ice 5 min, spread the whole mix on a pre-warmed LB + ampicillin (100 µg/mL) plate. Inducing to high copy number Grow a 5 mL overnight (LB + antibiotic) from a colony. Dilute the overnight 1:10 to read OD, then dilute to OD₆₀₀ 0.2 in LB + antibiotic + 1× CopyCutter Induction Solution (supplied at 1000×). Shake vigorously at 37 °C for 4 h. Aeration matters: use at least 15 mL tubes for 5 mL cultures and 125 mL flasks for 50 mL. Isolate plasmid DNA by your usual method. Screen clones by PCR while uninduced (few copies per cell). See also the FAQ on toxic genes.

Purpose Cre recombinase recognizes lox sites and joins the DNA back together, removing the sequence between them. Use this to remove an antibiotic-resistance cassette that is flanked by lox sites, for example one left at a deletion locus after recombineering. The example below assumes a strain with a lox-flanked zeocin-resistance cassette (zeoR) at the deletion site and a second, different marker elsewhere (nourseothricin resistance, nuoR, on an integrated plasmid), plus a kanamycin-marked Cre plasmid that also carries sacB. Remove the cassette Miniprep the Cre-sacB plasmid from E. coli and transform it into the strain (electroporation). Plate on kanamycin. Patch colonies on both LB + nourseothricin and LB + zeocin plates. You are looking for colonies that are nuoR and zeoS, which have lost the cassette. Cure the Cre plasmid Grow nuoR zeoS colonies in 7H9 + nourseothricin 20 µg/mL. Do not passage the culture to lose the plasmid. Passaging risks suppressor mutations in the mutants. Streak the culture on 10% sucrose plates (counter-selecting sacB). Patch colonies on both LB + kanamycin and LB + nourseothricin. You are looking for colonies that are kanS and nuoR.

M. smegmatis doubles in about 2.75 h, so pulses range from 10 min (short) to 90 min (long). Do the whole workflow in one day. Reagents Sterile 7H9 (+ Tween 80 + glycerol) with OADC or ADC Azide reagent (6-azido-trehalose, D-Ala-azide) Alkyne dye (AZDye 555 Alkyne for copper-catalyzed; AZDye 568 DBCO for copper-free) 1× PBS; DMSO Cu(II)SO₄·5H₂O, BTTP (use BTTP for live cells), sodium ascorbate (fresh each day) Optional: 4% PFA in PBS; PBS + 0.05% Tween 80 Stock solutions Alkyne dye: 10 mM in DMSO, –20 °C 1000× BTTP: 400 mM in DMSO (172.22 mg/mL), –20 °C 1000× Cu(II)SO₄·5H₂O: 200 mM in PBS (49.92 mg/mL) 100× sodium ascorbate: 120 mM in PBS (23.77 mg/mL); make only a small volume, good for one day 100× catalyst: mix BTTP and Cu(II) 1:1 at least 20 min before use and dilute with PBS (e.g. 20 µL 1000× Cu + 20 µL 1000× BTTP + 60 µL PBS = 100 µL). Stable at –20 °C for at least 1 month. Labeling (1 mL cultures) Start with mid-log cells (OD₆₀₀ 0.3–0.6). Spin 2 mL and resuspend in 1 mL fresh 7H9 + Tween to concentrate. Put 1 mL in each of two tubes. Add azide reagent (typically 100 µM–10 mM; here 1 mM 6-azido-trehalose from a 100 mM stock, 10 µL) to the experimental tube and 10 µL DMSO to the control. Incubate for the chosen pulse at 37 °C, 200 rpm. Spin 5,000 × g, 5 min (be consistent about hinge orientation). Sterile technique is no longer needed. Wash twice with 500 µL PBS + 0.05% Tween 80 (5,000 × g, 3 min). Resuspend in PBS + 0.05% Tween 80 so each reaction has 100 µL of cells (e.g. 300 µL for three samples). Keep OD₆₀₀ below 1.0 to avoid clumping. CuAAC reaction (100 µL) Prepare every reagent first. Order and timing matter. Cells in 100 µL PBS (± Tween). Add 0.25 µL alkyne dye (25 µM final). Add 1 µL premixed 100× catalyst (200 µM Cu(II), 400 µM BTTP final). Add 1 µL fresh sodium ascorbate (1.2 mM final), as soon as possible after the copper. Leave caps open. Mix with a brief flick; the dye should be evenly distributed. Stir/shake at 25 °C, ~500 rpm, 15 min. Spin 5,000 × g, 5 min. Wash three times with 500 µL PBS. If pellets are visibly dye-colored or controls are bright (non-specific staining), use PBS + 0.05% Tween 80 for the washes. Optional fixation Resuspend in 1.6% PFA, 10 min at room temperature, spin, wash once with PBS + 0.05% Tween 80. Downstream Microscopy: image as for other labeled cells. Flow cytometry: resuspend in 100 µL PBS + 0.05% Tween 80 + 0.5% FBS in a V-bottom 96-well plate. Plate reader: resuspend in 100 µL PBS in a U-bottom 96-well plate. Always include a DMSO-only (no azide) control and a no-dye control.

Follow your institution’s biosafety rules. M. smegmatis and E. coli K-12 strains are BSL-1; S. aureus, BCG and auxotrophic M. tuberculosis are BSL-2 (biosafety cabinet, appropriate PPE and waste handling). General steps (all organisms) Streak from the frozen stock onto an agar plate to get single colonies. Scrape the surface of the frozen stock with a sterile tip or loop; do not thaw the stock. Incubate until colonies appear (see the table). Pick a single colony into liquid medium with appropriate antibiotics. Keep the tube loosely capped or in a vented tube for aeration. Grow with aeration (shaking or rolling) at 37 °C. Use at mid-log phase (OD₆₀₀ ~0.4–0.8) for most experiments. Do not let cultures sit in stationary phase unless the experiment requires it. Make freezer stocks from fresh cultures by mixing with sterile glycerol (final 15–25%) and freezing at –80 °C. See Strain annotation and freezing. Key differences E. coli S. aureus M. smegmatis Biosafety BSL-1 (K-12) BSL-2 BSL-1 Doubling time (rich medium) ~20–30 min ~30–40 min about 3 h Colonies on plates overnight overnight (16–24 h) 3–4 days Liquid medium LB TSB or BHI 7H9 + ADC (or OADC) + glycerol + 0.05% Tween 80 Plate medium LB agar TSA 7H10/7H11 + supplements, or LB Saturated culture overnight overnight 2–3 days Clumping no clusters, grape-like yes, without detergent Aeration shake, 200–250 rpm shake, 200–250 rpm roller or shake, ~200 rpm Detergent none none Tween 80 (0.05%) to limit clumping Stationary-phase storage 4 °C for days 4 °C for days room temp or 4 °C; recover in fresh medium Inducible systems arabinose, IPTG anhydrotetracycline (Tet), cadmium anhydrotetracycline (Tet), acetamide, see Induction systems Mycobacteria Tween 80 (or tyloxapol) prevents clumping. It also slightly changes the cell surface, so keep the concentration constant between comparisons and use detergent-free medium only when the experiment needs it. Do not add Tween to plates. Growth is slow. Plan multi-day cultures. Starting a dense preculture the day before lets you set up experiments with log-phase cells. Do not over-dilute. Very low-density mycobacterial cultures grow poorly; inoculate at OD₆₀₀ 0.01–0.05 or more. Contamination from faster-growing bacteria is the biggest risk with long incubations. Antibiotics for the plasmid can protect against it, and cycloheximide or other additions are sometimes used. Seal plates in bags for long incubations. BCG and M. tuberculosis need OADC (not ADC) and take 3–4 weeks to form colonies. See Strains and growth. S. aureus This column is general microbiology knowledge and has not been checked against a lab protocol. Grows quickly in rich medium; include antibiotics for plasmid selection, e.g. erythromycin or chloramphenicol, according to the marker. Grows in clusters, so vortex or pipette before reading OD, and expect OD to be noisier than for rods. Make sure the medium is well aerated: use a flask volume at least 5× the culture volume. Handle as BSL-2: biosafety cabinet for open work, and decontaminate waste. E. coli For toxic constructs, grow at 30 °C or lower and avoid long overnights; see the FAQ. For plasmid preps, use a fresh overnight in antibiotic. For competent cells see Electrocompetent cells and chemical transformation. M. marinum Handle at the biosafety level required by your institution. Wild-type strain: buy the M strain from ATCC. Grow a first passage (P1) and make P1 stocks, then expand to a large P2 culture. Make freezer stocks from P2 and distribute these as the parental strain to lab members. Do not passage the strain unnecessarily. It does not lose PDIM, but it can lose its ability to lyse red blood cells, so a new P1 may be needed every few years. Medium: 7H9 with Tween 80. OADC can be added, but it is expensive and not required. Plasmids: many are derived from pMV306 (L5-integrating); L5 integrating plasmids work. Fast-cloning genes behind the MOP promoter complements well. In general, anything that works in M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis works in M. marinum. Transformation: electroporation as in Mycobacteria Protocols (Parish and Roberts, eds.); glycine in the culture improves efficiency. M. marinum needs more DNA than M. tuberculosis (about 1 µg or more). See Knockouts in M. marinum. Knockouts: p2NIL/pGOAL with a UV step for the DNA (essential; without it, plasmids integrate at the wrong site). Temperature: M. marinum grows best at about 30–32 °C rather than 37 °C. Confirm growth temperature for your strain. Cryovial labels To print labels instead of writing on cryovials by hand, use the label template: download the cryovial label template (.docx). Print on the label stock your lab uses (the template is formatted for ToughTag cryovial labels), fill in strain/plasmid, date and initials before printing, and match the information to the freezer-stock database (Strain annotation and freezing). Antibiotics Use the concentrations in Antibiotic plates for E. coli and mycobacteria. Concentrations for S. aureus are different and strain-dependent. Verify S. aureus antibiotic concentrations and media before use.

Immunoprecipitation (Turapov et al.) Couple anti-CwlM antibody to CNBr-activated Sepharose 4B (a resin for immobilizing ligands containing primary amines) following the manufacturer’s coupling protocol. Mix 1 mL containing 100 µg protein from a cell fraction (e.g. membrane or cytosol) with 10 µL antibody–Sepharose. Rotate for 60 min. Spin 500 × g for 5 min. Discard supernatant and wash the resin 3× with TBS. Elute with 40 µL phosphoric acid, pH 2.0. The original method does not say how the eluate is neutralized or dried before blotting/mass spec. Control: the same fraction from a CwlM-depleted mutant. To test candidate partners directly, mix recombinant CwlM with 10 µg of each purified candidate in phosphate buffer (20 mM KH₂PO₄ pH 7.0, 100 mM NaCl, 10 mM KCl) with 10 µL antibody–Sepharose, and process as above. Suggested gel layout: ladder; CwlM; CwlM + resin FT; CwlM + resin eluate; partner; partner + resin FT; partner + resin eluate; partner + CwlM + resin FT; partner + CwlM + resin eluate. DHFR two-hybrid (M-PFC): plates and controls M-PFC splits mycobacterial dihydrofolate reductase into fragments fused to the two proteins; if the proteins interact, DHFR is reconstituted and cells grow on trimethoprim (TMP). Turapov et al. Used here Plates 7H10 7H11 (clearer results than 7H10 in testing) Antibiotics Hyg 50, Kan 50, TMP 15 Hyg 50, Kan 25, TMP 50 Make plates ± TMP. Streak controls on both: Negative: vectors expressing DHFR fragments with no interaction domain. Should grow on –TMP and not on +TMP. Positive: vectors carrying GCN4 leucine-zipper domains (which dimerize). Should grow on both. Test both 7H10 and 7H11. Proceed with the medium that gives the clearest separation. Cloning plan for the test proteins Amplify each ORF from M. tuberculosis genomic DNA with primers designed for each vector (separate primer pairs for each of the four vectors). Gel-purify the PCR products (Gel purification). A longer incubation of the gel slice in dissolving buffer (1–3 h at ~54 °C) can increase yield. Prepare four parent vectors by miniprep and digest (40–50 µg DNA each, then column cleanup, resuspend 30–50 µL, NanoDrop): pUAB100 (BamHI + ClaI), pUAB200 (MfeI + ClaI), pUAB300 (BamHI + HpaI), pUAB400 (MfeI + HpaI). Assemble by Gibson (Gibson assembly), calculating insert and vector volumes. Letting the reaction proceed overnight at room temperature can help. Transform ~5 µL into E. coli. For electrocompetent cells, dialyze the Gibson reaction 15–20 min first and use 1–2 µL. Run the remaining ~5 µL on a TAE gel to judge success. Pick 16–32 colonies per plate, patch them, and colony-PCR with check primers (Colony PCR). Sequence 2–3 positive clones. If colony PCR is inconclusive, miniprep 8 colonies and do an analytical digest (0.5–1.5 µg). Strain names and primer names from the working notes have been removed. Expected band sizes were not recorded in the source.

Mix: 1 mL DNA ladder 1 mL TE buffer pH 7.4 1 mL 6× loading dye 3 mL nuclease-free water Mix gently by pipetting. Make six 1 mL aliquots and store at –20 °C. Load 6 µL per lane. Check the dilution against the ladder’s concentration; the same recipe may not suit every ladder.

Purpose Introduce a plasmid or assembly reaction (for example a Gibson or ligation product) into chemically competent E. coli, and test how competent a new batch of cells is. Transformation Competent cells (DH5α, Mach1, TOP10 or XL1-Blue) are stored in 100 µL aliquots at −80 °C. Split one tube between two or three transformations if you are doing several at a time. Thaw competent cells on ice. Add 5–10 µL of assembly or ligation reaction. Incubate on ice 15–20 min. Heat shock at 42 °C for 45–60 seconds. Return to ice for 2 min. Add 1 mL LB and incubate at 37 °C for 45–60 min. Spin the tube and remove the LB. Resuspend the pellet in 100 µL LB and spread on an LB plate with the appropriate antibiotic. Incubate at 37 °C overnight. If your gene may be toxic Grow the recovery at 30 °C for about 1.5 hours and incubate the plate at 30 °C overnight. Colonies take 24+ hours but are often correct, with little background. TOP10 and XL1-Blue (which carries a tet repressor) tend to suit toxic cloning, but both grow more slowly than DH5α. Testing transformation efficiency Use a control plasmid with a known concentration, aliquoted at 100 ng. Transform 100 ng of plasmid into chemically competent cells with the heat-shock protocol above. Add 200 µL LB and recover for 45 min at 37 °C. Make a 10-fold dilution series (tubes labeled 10⁻¹ to 10⁻⁶), each with 270 µL LB. Move 30 µL from the transformation into the 10⁻¹ tube, mix by pipetting, and continue down the series with a fresh tip each time. Plate about 270 µL of the remaining undiluted transformation and of each dilution on separate selection plates. Count colonies on the lowest-dilution plate with individual, countable colonies. Colonies per aliquot = colonies × 10^(dilution). For example, 57 colonies on the 10⁻⁵ plate gives 57 × 10⁵. This ignores the fraction of the transformation plated: if the total volume after recovery is about 310 µL (100 µL cells + 10 µL plasmid + 200 µL LB) and you plate 270 µL, multiply by about 1.15 for an exact value. The correction is small relative to the order-of-magnitude efficiency usually reported. Transformants per µg = total colonies × 10 (because 100 ng was used). Good competent cells give about 10⁶ colonies per µg or higher. Where it usually fails No or very few colonies. Test the efficiency of your competent cells with a control plasmid (above). Suspected toxic gene. Use the 30 °C recovery and incubation above, and a strain such as TOP10 or XL1-Blue.

Grow a starter culture overnight (add the appropriate antibiotic if you want to select against contaminants). In the morning, dilute to OD₆₀₀ of at least 0.05 in LB without antibiotics. Grow to OD₆₀₀ ~0.8 (up to 1.0 is fine). Pellet at 5,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. Pour off the supernatant. Wash 1: ice-cold sterile 10% glycerol, half the original culture volume. Resuspend well and pellet again as above. Wash 2: ice-cold 10% glycerol, a quarter of the original volume. Pellet again. Resuspend in enough ice-cold 10% glycerol to give 1/100 of the original culture volume (e.g. for 200 mL, use 1.5–1.75 mL to reach about 2 mL). Use fresh, or aliquot 50 µL, snap-freeze in a dry ice / 95% ethanol bath for 30 s and store at –80 °C. Keep cells and tubes cold throughout. See Electrocompetent cells and electroporation for settings.

E. coli electrocompetent cells Grow a starter culture. It can include the antibiotic to which the strain is resistant to select out contaminants (for XL1-Blue, tetracycline at 10 µg/mL). Dilute to an OD of at least 0.05 in LB without antibiotic. Grow to an OD of about 0.8 (up to 1.0 is fine). Spin at 5,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C and pour off the supernatant. Wash twice in ice-cold sterile 10% glycerol: first in half the original volume, then in a quarter. Keep the cells cold. Resuspend the final pellet in ice-cold 10% glycerol to a final volume of one-hundredth the original (for a 200 mL culture, use 1.5–1.75 mL glycerol to make 2 mL). Aliquot 50 µL. Use fresh, or snap-freeze for 30 seconds in liquid nitrogen (or a dry ice/95% ethanol bath) and store at −80 °C. M. smegmatis electrocompetent cells Cells made this way have an efficiency of about 10⁴–10⁵ CFU/µg DNA. One vial can be split for up to 4 transformations. Use a log-phase culture (10 mL is ideal). Pour into a 15 mL conical tube. Keep cells and 10% glycerol on ice. Spin at 5,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. Remove the supernatant and resuspend in 10 mL 10% glycerol. Resuspending first in 1 mL with a pipette and then adding 9 mL saves supplies. Vortex briefly; keep the cells cold. Spin again at 5,000 × g for 10 min. Repeat the glycerol wash 2–3 times in total. Wash in 10% glycerol, not water. Resuspend the final pellet in 200 µL 10% glycerol. Add 1 µL vector to 200 µL cells in a cuvette and electroporate (settings below). The desired pulse time is about 3 ms. Keep on ice while preparing 1 mL of 7H9, then recover in 7H9 for 2–3 hours. Spin at 14,000 × g for 30–60 seconds, remove the supernatant, resuspend in 200 µL 7H9, and plate on LB with antibiotic using beads. BCG and M. tuberculosis Make competent cells fresh each time to prevent arcing, following the M. smegmatis procedure. Resuspend at the end in 8/100 of the starting volume (for a 100 mL culture, 8 mL, not 1 mL) and use 400 µL of cells per transformation. Use a different electroporation setting from M. smegmatis and E. coli. Electroporator settings Organism Voltage Resistance Capacitance E. coli and M. smegmatis (standard transformation) 2500 V 125 Ω 25 µF BCG 2500 V 725 Ω 50 µF M. smegmatis recombineering (linear DNA) 2500 V 1000 Ω 25 µF Standard transformation and recombineering use different resistances. For standard transformation the desired pulse time is about 3 ms; for recombineering the time constant should be 20–30 ms. Where it usually fails Arcing. Make BCG/M. tuberculosis competent cells fresh each time. Low efficiency. Wash in glycerol, not water, for mycobacteria, and keep E. coli cells cold throughout.

Day 1 Set up overnight cultures in 5 mL 7H9, diluted so that they reach OD₆₀₀ ~0.6 by the planned morning time. Day 2 Take 1 mL culture. Pellet (16,000 × g, 1 min, room temperature) and wash twice in PBS + 0.05% Tween 80. Resuspend in 1 mL PBS + Tween 80. Add ethidium bromide to 2 µg/mL. In a black 96-well plate, add 4.5 µL nanopure water to every well that will receive culture. Add 195.5 µL bacterial suspension in triplicate (200 µL final). Track the wells carefully. Plate reader: 37 °C, no shaking, excitation 520 nm, emission 560–640 nm. Read every 60 s for 90 min. Express fluorescence as the percent increase over each sample’s value at 1 min. 2 µg/mL EtBr should be below the MIC for M. smegmatis and should not itself reduce viability. If a mutant might be hypersusceptible, determine the EtBr MIC first. Permeability with an antibiotic (example: meropenem) Thaw a 10 mg/mL meropenem stock and vortex. Overnight cultures at OD ~0.4. Dilute to OD 0.1 in 10 mL fresh 7H9. Prepare two sets, (+) and (−) antibiotic. Add meropenem at ½ MIC of the wild-type strain: value to be filled in to (+). Incubate at 37 °C on a roller. Run the permeability assay (steps 1–6) at 0, 3 and 6 h. At each time point take 1 mL, wash three times, normalize all resuspensions to the same OD (measure each time), and scale the EtBr volume to the final resuspension volume. Alternative settings (filter-based reader) Excitation filter 530 nm, emission filter 590 nm, 570 nm dichroic mirror; black 96-well plate; no shaking; room temperature; 30 min duration; reading every 15 s.

Warning: fixation can alter cell shape and the distribution of fluorophore-tagged molecules. For a final experiment, test that fixation does not affect the phenomenon you are studying. Fixation is best for trial runs or when live imaging is not possible. Do not leave fixed cells in the fridge for more than one night; they fall apart. Requirements: PBS-Tween (1× PBS + 0.05% Tween 80) and 16% PFA (a handling and storage guide is in your institution’s chemical safety rules; PFA is toxic, work in a hood). Pellet the culture (5,000 rpm, 5 min, clinical centrifuge). Discard supernatant. Resuspend in 1 mL PBS-Tween and move to a labeled microcentrifuge tube. Add 100 µL 16% PFA (about 1.5% final). Invert to mix. Leave 10 min on the bench. Spin about 1 min at maximum speed in a microcentrifuge. Resuspend in 1 mL PBS-Tween. Keep at 4 °C until imaging (no more than one night). For probe-labeled cells see Probe labeling; image settings in HADA/NADA staining.

Purpose Recover a PCR product or digested vector from an agarose gel for cloning. Expect to lose a large fraction of the DNA: about 80–90% in kit-based gel purification in this lab’s experience. Option 1: low-melt agarose (fast, works well for Gibson assembly) Pour a 1% TAE gel with low-melt agarose instead of regular agarose. It takes about 2 hours to set at room temperature, so you may want to put the rig in the fridge after pouring. Run your vector and inserts and cut out the bands. Handle the gel carefully; it falls apart more easily than a regular gel. Warm the slices for a few minutes at 60 °C, vortex, and pipette 1–2 µL of the melted gel solution directly into the tube with the Gibson enzymes. Option 2: column kit (for example Promega Wizard SV Gel and PCR Clean-Up) Cut out the gel slice and add Membrane Binding Solution. Incubate at 50–60 °C for 2–3 hours, vortexing for 1–2 minutes every 30 minutes until the gel is fully dissolved. Resuspend, transfer the dissolved gel to the minicolumn and leave it on the bench for 10 minutes. Follow the kit protocol for the remaining steps. To elute, add 30–50 µL elution buffer or nuclease-free water to the filter, leave 10 minutes, and centrifuge at 16,000 × g for 1 minute. PCR products and digests, and changes from the manufacturer’s protocol For PCR products, add an equal volume of Membrane Binding Solution to the reaction. The manufacturer’s instructions are in Promega Technical Bulletin TB308 (www.promega.com). The lab changes to that protocol are: After adding the dissolved gel mixture or prepared sample to the minicolumn, incubate at room temperature for 10 minutes (the printed protocol says 1 minute). For elution, add 50 µL nuclease-free water, incubate at room temperature for 10 minutes (printed: 1 minute), then centrifuge at 16,000 × g for 1 minute. For a vector digest: add Membrane Binding Solution directly to the overnight digestion (5 µL, including 1 µL from the phosphatase step), resuspend very well, and add to the column straight away. Where it usually fails Very low yield. Expected losses are high; the low-melt method is faster for Gibson assembly, and eluting in 30 µL rather than 50 µL gives a more concentrated product. Gel slice not dissolving. Keep vortexing at the stated intervals during the 2–3 hour incubation.

Overview PCR and gel purification of the insert. Restriction digest and column purification of the vector. Add insert and vector to a 5 µL Gibson master-mix aliquot for a final volume of 10 µL. Incubate at 50 °C for 1 hour. Transform 5 µL of the reaction into chemically competent E. coli (protocol). Plate and screen colonies (colony PCR). Gibson assembly uses an exonuclease to create long, thermodynamically stable single-stranded overhangs at 50 °C. It is not a homologous recombination method. Primer design The overlap between fragments must be long enough that its melting temperature is above 50 °C. As a fast rule, use 60 nt primers: 20 nt that anneal to the template and 40 nt (including any restriction site) that overlap the vector. This is overkill but works at a very high rate. If you need to add something (an epitope tag, a restriction site), subtract the required bases from the overhang, keeping the overhang melting temperature above 50 °C. Overlaps of about 30 nt work, and some people routinely use about 20 nt. Primers under 60 nt allow the smallest IDT order size; longer primers (up to 90 nt) have also worked. For several fragments, design primers so adjacent fragments overlap with a melting temperature above 50 °C; about 40 nt is a good default. PCR (Q5 polymerase example) Ingredient Amount (µL) ddH₂O 25.5 Primer 1 (100 µM) 1 Primer 2 (100 µM) 1 dNTPs (10 mM each) 1 Q5 reaction buffer 10 Q5 GC enhancer 10 Template 1 Q5 polymerase 0.5 Primer amounts can be reduced substantially; extra does no harm. Program: 98 °C 0:30; 35 cycles of 98 °C 0:30, 60 °C 0:30, 72 °C 0:30 per kb of product; 72 °C 2:00; hold at 4 °C. Vector restriction digest Use standard methods with any suitable enzyme(s). A single-enzyme digest works for Gibson without phosphatase treatment. Overnight digestion is preferred; a couple of hours has worked in a pinch. Purification Column-purify the vector with a standard PCR/enzyme clean-up kit. Gel-purify the PCR product, or see gel purification. Gibson reaction The reaction tolerates a wide range of vector and insert amounts. Aliquot the Gibson reagent (NEB) into 5 µL 2X reactions in PCR tubes. A typical reaction adds 2 µL vector and 3 µL insert for 10 µL total. The nominal ideal is 100 ng vector with a 3:1 insert:vector ratio, but measuring this exactly is usually unnecessary. Include a negative control with vector only (water in place of insert) to control for residual restriction and ligation. Incubate 1 hour at 50 °C. Transform 5 µL of the raw reaction directly into chemically competent E. coli, recover and plate. There should be several-fold more colonies with insert than in the negative control. Pick about 3 colonies and screen by restriction digest or colony PCR. Multiple inserts Efficiency falls with each additional insert. Up to three inserts at once has worked, though one or two is best. With more inserts (or after a failed multi-insert reaction), first do a Gibson reaction with all inserts but no vector. Add 1 µL of the raw reaction to a new PCR with the two terminal primers to make a single pre-assembled fragment, purify it as for a single insert, then use it in the final Gibson reaction with vector. Where it usually fails PCR fails. Run a gradient PCR with 8 tubes (one strip) across annealing temperatures of 50–70 °C. Few or no colonies with more than two fragments. Pre-assemble the inserts as described above. Insert and vector-only control have similar colony counts. The vector may not be fully cut or purified; check the digest.

Enter data in Prism: X = elapsed time; Y = three replicate values in side-by-side sub-columns. Make a new table with a single replicate per data set, called “singles”, and copy the data and times into it. Plot the singles data and set the Y axis to log₂ scale. Exclude the non-linear parts (lag and stationary phase). Only log-phase measurements should be used to calculate doubling time. Look at each biological replicate separately, note which time points are linear, and exclude the rest (highlight, Cmd+E; the table must be frozen). Fit each replicate: Analyze → Nonlinear regression → Exponential growth equation. Take the doubling times from the results table into a new column table (replicates in columns; use “paste transpose” if needed). Aim for at least 3 biological replicates per strain or condition. Compare strains: Analyze → Ordinary one-way ANOVA → Multiple comparisons → compare the mean of each column with the mean of a control column (set the control to wild type). Use biological, not technical, replicates as n. See Growth curve setup and Manual growth curves.

Purpose Start every well of a plate-reader growth curve at the same initial OD₆₀₀ by diluting each culture into medium. The calculator below gives the volumes of culture and 7H9 for each strain. The default is 200 µL final volume and an initial OD of 0.1. Calculator Final volume per well (µL) Initial OD₆₀₀ # Strain / genotype Culture OD₆₀₀ Culture (µL) 7H9 (µL) Culture volume = (initial OD × final volume) ÷ culture OD. Medium volume = final volume − culture volume. If a culture’s OD is below the target, it cannot be diluted to the target and the row shows “OD too low”. Plate reader settings (temperature, shaking, reading interval, duration) and plate layout notes to be added.

These columns are for native purification only. They connect to any low-pressure chromatography system with 10-32 fittings. Maximum pressure 72 psi; not autoclavable; storage in 20% ethanol or 2% benzyl alcohol at 4 °C. Buffers (manufacturer’s recommendations) Solution Composition Lysis / wash 150 mM NaCl, 10 mM Na₂HPO₄, 5 mM EDTA, pH 7.4 Elution 20 mM glutathione, 100 mM Tris, 5 mM EDTA, pH 8.0 Desalting 137 mM NaCl, 2.7 mM KCl, 4.3 mM Na₂HPO₄, 8.1 mM KH₂PO₄, pH 7.4 Cleaning 1 500 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris, pH 8.0 Cleaning 2 500 mM NaCl, 100 mM sodium acetate, pH 4.5 Storage 2% benzyl alcohol or 20% ethanol Compatible additives include up to 5 mM DTT, 30 mM β-mercaptoethanol, 5% non-ionic detergents, 20% glycerol and 2 M NaCl (see the manual’s compatibility table). Quick solubility screen Pellet ~2 mL E. coli culture (4,000 × g, 10 min, 4 °C). Resuspend in 500 µL PBS, sonicate 60 s on ice in 10 s pulses. Keep 50 µL as Total. Spin 12,000 × g, 10 min, 4 °C. Keep 50 µL of the supernatant as Soluble. Resuspend the pellet in 500 µL 6 M urea in PBS, sonicate, spin, and keep 50 µL as Insoluble. Add 150 µL Laemmli to each, boil 5 min, and load 10 µL on a gel. Lysate preparation Harvest at 8,000 × g for 10 min, 4 °C. Weigh the pellet and resuspend in 10 volumes lysis/wash buffer (200 mL of culture gives ~0.8–1 g; 200 mL suits a 1 mL column and 1 L a 5 mL column for highly expressed protein). Optional: DNase (100 U/mL) or Benzonase (25 U/mL), 10 min at room temperature, to reduce viscosity. Sonicate on ice (25% output) 4 × 1 min. Spin 16,000 × g, 20 min, 4 °C. Filter the supernatant (0.45 µm). Freezing once at –20 °C is possible but can allow proteolysis; re-filter after thawing. Purification (1 mL column; scale flow rates for a 5 mL column) Step Volume 1 mL column 5 mL column Flush storage solution 2 CV water or buffer 2 mL/min 10 mL/min Equilibrate 5 CV 2 mL/min 10 mL/min Load lysate 5–10 CV 0.5–1 mL/min 2.5–5 mL/min Wash 12 CV 2 mL/min 10 mL/min Elute 3 CV 0.5 mL/min 2.5 mL/min Collect fractions, run an SDS-PAGE gel, and pool the clean ones. Cleaning and storage 5 CV cleaning solution 1 and 5 CV cleaning solution 2 at 2 mL/min; rinse with 5 CV water; 5 CV storage solution at 1 mL/min. Seal and store at 4 °C. Dynamic binding capacity More than 11 mg per mL of resin (for a 51 kDa GST fusion at 0.5 mL/min; depends on pH, flow rate and temperature). Also see His-tag purification overview and Test inductions.

Part 1: HADA pulse (stop here if not doing the chase) Grow a 5 mL culture to log phase. Pellet all 5 mL at 5,000 × g for 10 min. Resuspend in 3 mL 7H9 (+ antibiotics if used). Add 3 µL HADA (1:1000) and incubate 15 min. Pellet 1 mL at a time in 1.5 mL tubes, 16,000 × g for 90 s. Resuspend thoroughly in 3 mL 7H9, then pellet again (1 mL per tube, 16,000 × g, 90 s). Part 2: Outgrowth and NADA pulse Resuspend cells in 1 mL 7H9 and add to 4 mL 7H9 (final 5 mL), with antibiotics if used. Measure and record OD₆₀₀. Incubate 90 min at 37 °C on a roller. Stain 1 mL of culture with 1 µL NADA (1:1000) for 2 min at room temperature. Pellet at 16,000 × g for 90 s. Resuspend in 7H9. Start with 100 µL and add 50 µL at a time until the suspension is not too turbid. Image (example settings below). Filter Exposure Lamp power GFP (NADA) 100 ms 30% DAPI (HADA) 700 ms 40% DIA to be confirmed 50% Settings depend on the microscope and need to be tuned for each setup. Notes Image fixed cells within 24 h of fixation. For a lone HADA stain, stop after Part 1. Measurement of old- and new-pole length from the images is done in Fiji with a segmented-line macro; a separate analysis page will be added.

Overview Plasmid: pET His-SUMO-CwlM, stored in a cloning strain. Miniprep the vector, then transform into chemically competent E. coli BL21 (Codon Plus) each time and use a single colony for the starter. Select with ampicillin (140 µg/mL) in LB. 1. Expression Induce 1L of culture with 1.3 mM IPTG at 18 °C overnight with shaking (220 rpm, in 4L flask). Pellet at 5,000 [rpm] for 20 min and store pellets at –20 °C. Record OD₆₀₀ before and after induction and keep 50–100 µL of each in Laemmli buffer to confirm induction on a gel. 2. Lysis (sonication) Wash buffer: 50 mM Tris pH 8, 350 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT (add fresh). Thaw pellets on ice and resuspend in 20–50 mL wash buffer. Add a pinch of lysozyme; 30 min on ice. Sonicate 35 s at 40% amplitude, 30 s rests, 15 cycles. Spin 13,000 rpm, 25 min. Keep samples of supernatant and (resuspended) pellet in Laemmli. 3. Ni-NTA by FPLC Use filtered, degassed buffers. If the supernatant is cloudy, syringe-filter it before loading. Equilibrate: 1.25 CV wash buffer Wash: 3 CV wash buffer, then a 1.25 CV gradient 0–100% elution buffer Elute: 3 CV elution buffer (wash buffer with 250 mM imidazole) 4. Check fractions Run flow-through, wash and elution fractions with supernatant and pellet samples on a 12% SDS gel. His-SUMO-CwlM runs at ~56 kDa. 5. Dialysis Dialyze the eluate overnight against wash/elution buffer with no imidazole. 6. Size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) NanoDrop the dialyzed protein (blank: dialysis buffer) and keep a gel sample. Load on SEC in 50 mM Tris pH 8, 350 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT (equilibrate 1.25 CV; elute 1.25 CV). Run fractions on a gel, pool the clean ones, concentrate to 1 mg/mL at least, NanoDrop to confirm , adjust glycerol to 10% final, re-measure, flash freeze 10-100 µL aliquots using liquid nitrogen and store at –80 °C. Amplitude of sonication, centrifuge speeds as rpm and the aliquot/freezing step need future experimental confirmation.

Taking images Use the same settings (bit depth, exposure time, light intensity) for samples that will be compared. Always check for saturation. Do not take saturated images. Check several images across a comparison set when choosing settings. Use 16-bit images if some samples saturate. Saving images Save image sets in dated folders that can be matched to pages in your lab notebook. Processing images Representative cells: do the quantitative analysis first, then choose cells that represent the result. Adjustments: adjust images being compared in exactly the same way. Cropping and figures: Crop from images with the same scaling. Do not change the crop size while assembling the figure; make the figure file larger instead. Use the ROI manager to keep crop sizes consistent. Use white outlines to show where separate images are joined. Include a scale bar. Only after all crops and scale bars are in place, scale the whole figure together (for example in Illustrator). Keep original, unprocessed files. Raw images for blots follow the same principle: Western blot.

Radioactivity: work only in an approved radioisotope area, with training, shielding, monitoring and waste procedures from your institution’s radiation safety office. Set-up Kinase buffer: 50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 250 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol. Use a kinase:substrate mass ratio of 1:10 (5 µg substrate to 0.5 µg kinase per 20 µL reaction). Thaw one aliquot of each protein on ice. Measure the concentration of each with the kinase buffer as blank. Label tubes. Example set for testing a substrate against two kinases: substrate only (no-kinase negative control), one for each substrate kinase + known substrate (positive controls, e.g. PknA–Wag31, PknB–CwlM) PknA + test substrate PknB + test substrate PknA + PknB + test substrate Add MnCl₂ to 1 mM final (0.8 µL of a 25 mM stock into 20 µL). Add the volume of each protein that gives the desired mass (µg ÷ mg/mL = µL) and kinase buffer to 20 µL total. Worked example: 5 µg of substrate at 10 mg/mL = 0.5 µL; 0.5 µg of kinase at 4.2 mg/mL = 0.12 µL. In the radioactive area, add hot ATP at 0.182 µCi/µL final: prepare a mixture of 3 µL hot ATP + 5.5 µL kinase buffer and add 1 µL to each tube. Isotope, stock activity and µCi per reaction need to be filled in. Incubate 30 min at room temperature. Immediately add 5 µL 6× Laemmli. Do not heat. Gel and imaging Load 10 µL on a 12% SDS-PAGE gel. Run about 50 min at 35 mA, then 45 mA. Run the dye front off the gel, so that unincorporated ATP runs out and does not blow out the signal. Stain for 1 h, destain 2–3 h, and photograph the gel. Sandwich the gel between two sheets of clear filter paper wetted with 40% ethanol (prevents cracking). Squeegee out bubbles, clamp between plastic sheets and dry in a hood overnight. Blank a phosphor screen by placing it white side against a light box for ~1 h. Cut the plastic to fit, place the dried gel against the white side of the screen in the cassette, oriented right-side up, and label the cassette (name, date). Expose overnight (about 8 h can suffice) and scan on a phosphorimager. Controls Include substrate-only, kinase-only (autophosphorylation) and known kinase–substrate pairs. Compare the autoradiograph to the stained gel to confirm that the signal is at the substrate band.

Inducible expression Tet-ON (anhydrotetracycline, aTc). aTc turns expression on of genes cloned downstream of the TetO promoter. Maximal induction is at about 100 ng/mL. aTc is light sensitive; cover tubes with foil for storage and time courses. One-plasmid systems use hygromycin with pUVTetOR or pTetSG; two-plasmid systems combine hygromycin and kanamycin with pTetO and pMC1. The system is used with doxycycline as inducer in mice. Nitrile (pNIT). Caprolactam or isovaleronitrile (IVN) turn on genes downstream of the NitA-dependent promoter via the NitA activator. A single-plasmid system. M. tuberculosis uses caprolactam; M. smegmatis is induced with IVN at a 10⁻⁶ or 10⁻⁷ dilution of a main stock (about 1–10 µM). NitA is somewhat toxic: cells filament a little and grow slowly after induction. Although published as equivalent, pNIT induces less than the Tet system. Acetamide. The inducer is acetamide, an amide, acting on the acetamidase promoter. A single-plasmid system. There is conflicting evidence for leaky expression from the uninduced promoter. Depletion Tet promoter replacement. The native promoter is replaced by an aTc-inducible promoter, commonly by homologous recombination or recombineering. The gene is depleted by diluting the strain into medium without aTc. Inducible degradation. The target is tagged with a degradation tag that is cleaved by an inducible HIV-2 protease, uncovering an ssrA signal recognized by Clp proteases. Adding aTc leads to target degradation.

M-PFC is not a magic bullet; it may fail for a given pair of proteins. Host strain: M. smegmatis mc²155. Vectors Vector Type Marker Contents pUAB100 episomal Hyg GCN4 homodimerization domain fused to the N-terminus of mDHFR fragment F[1,2] with a glycine linker; insert by replacing GCN4 (MscI/ClaI or BamHI/ClaI) pUAB200 integrative Kan GCN4 fused to mDHFR fragment F[3]; replace GCN4 with MunI/ClaI pUAB300 episomal Hyg mDHFR F[1,2] for in-frame fusion at its C-terminus, multiple cloning sites (preferred for libraries) pUAB400 integrative Kan mDHFR F[3] for in-frame fusion at its C-terminus Clone gene A in pUAB100 or pUAB300 and gene B in pUAB200 or pUAB400, in frame with the complementary DHFR fragment. Verify by sequencing. Assay Prepare competent M. smegmatis and check efficiency (10⁴–10⁵ transformants/µg). Electroporate both constructs. Recover 3 h at 37 °C in 1 mL 7H9. Plate the whole mix on 7H11 + Kan + Hyg. Incubate 3 days at 37 °C. Subculture transformants on 7H11 + Kan + Hyg + trimethoprim (30–50 µg/mL). Alternatively suspend a few colonies in 100 µL PBS and streak 10 µL. Incubate 4–5 days at 37 °C. Growth on trimethoprim indicates interaction. Stronger interactions grow earlier. Controls: pUAB100 + pUAB200 (GCN4 domains, strong interaction) as the positive control; any one of the clones with an unrelated partner as the negative control. Notes from the protocol Use 7H11, not 7H10 or 7H9 + agar. Do not change the Kan, Hyg or trimethoprim concentrations. For membrane proteins, use pUAB100 and pUAB200 and make sure the DHFR fragments sit in the cytoplasm. Some proteins need a free N- or C-terminus; test parallel and antiparallel orientations. Interaction strength can be measured with the Alamar Blue assay (Singh et al. 2006). Make fresh trimethoprim for plates; do not store trimethoprim plates long at 4 °C. Library screening (summary) An M. tuberculosis H37Rv library (partial AciI/HpaI digests, 0.5–2 kb, cloned in pUAB300; about 5 × 10⁵ independent clones with more than 90% cloning efficiency) is transformed into M. smegmatis carrying the bait (in pUAB200 or pUAB400). A semi-exhaustive screen needs about 30–60 electroporations (400 µL cells and 2–5 µg DNA each), plated on 7H11 + Kan + Hyg + trimethoprim (30 µg/mL), 4–8 days at 37 °C. Many trimethoprim-resistant colonies carry the M. tuberculosis dfrA gene (Rv2763c) itself; remove them by colony PCR with insert-flanking and dfrA primers. Identify real positives by colony PCR and sequencing, and re-test with an unrelated control. See also the DHFR two-hybrid cloning plan.

Beads: ferrimagnetic spheres coated with 6% agarose and Strep-Tactin XT, supplied as a 5% (v/v) suspension (20 µL = 1 µL beads). Capacity: up to 0.85 nmol tagged protein per µL beads (25.5 µg of a 30 kDa protein). The beads are not meant to be reused. Buffers (10× stocks; dilute 1:9 with water): Buffer W: 1 M Tris-Cl, 1.5 M NaCl, 10 mM EDTA, pH 8 (10×) Buffer BXT: Buffer W with 500 mM biotin (10×) Batch purification in tubes Cleared extract volume should not exceed 2.5 mL per µL beads, and the tagged protein should be above 1 mg/mL. If below this, the vendor recommends gravity-flow Strep-Tactin columns instead. 100 mM biotin can give a more concentrated eluate. Calculate beads: 1 µL beads per 0.85 nmol protein. Place the bead suspension in a tube, collect on a magnet, remove the supernatant. Equilibrate with 200 µL 1× Buffer W per µL beads, 3 times. Clear the sample (20 min at 10,000 × g, or 4,000 × g for small volumes). Resuspend the beads in the cleared sample. Incubate 30 min on ice, vortexing 3–4 times. Collect beads on the magnet; remove the supernatant (save the flow-through). Wash 3× with 100 µL 1× Buffer W per µL beads. Elute. Native: 25 µL 1× Buffer BXT per µL beads, 10 min with 2–3 vortexes; transfer the supernatant to a new tube; repeat once. The first elution gives the highest concentration. Denaturing: SDS sample buffer, 95 °C for 2 min. Strep-Tactin XT also denatures and appears as an extra band at ~13.5 kDa. Check purity by SDS-PAGE (Coomassie or silver) and quantify by Bradford with BSA as standard. Batch purification in 96-well plates For targets up to 90 kDa, at least 0.425 nmol per 200 µL sample. Use at least 40 µL of the 5% suspension per well (2 µL beads), equilibrate with 100 µL 1× Buffer W per µL beads, bind 60 min at room temperature on a plate shaker at 700 rpm, wash 3×, elute with 50 µL 1× Buffer BXT per µL beads (400 rpm, 10 min, twice). Troubleshooting (vendor) No or weak binding: add protease inhibitors and work at 2–8 °C; use a protease-deficient expression strain; move the tag to the other terminus or use a longer linker or Twin-Strep-tag. Contaminants: reduce with reducing agents (disulfide-linked), add salt (up to 5 M NaCl) or mild detergents (up to 2% Triton X-100 or Tween 20) for non-covalent ones, and use biotin blocking solution or avidin for biotinylated proteins. See also the Strep-Tactin pulldown.

Purpose Measure growth of a strain over time by sampling a culture and reading OD₆₀₀ by hand. Use this when you need to sample the culture itself (CFU, protein, RNA, microscopy), when volumes are too large for a plate, or to check a plate-reader result. For many strains in parallel, see Setting up a 96-well growth curve. Materials Starter culture in mid-log phase (see Culturing) Fresh pre-warmed medium: 7H9 (+ supplements, + Tween 80) for mycobacteria; TSB or LB for S. aureus; LB for E. coli Flasks (about 5–10× the culture volume) or culture tubes Spectrophotometer and cuvettes; medium for blanking Antibiotics or inducers as the experiment requires Procedure Prepare the starter. Grow an overnight (or, for slow mycobacteria, multi-day) culture to mid-log. Check that it is not clumped or contaminated. Choose the starting OD. Dilute into fresh medium to OD₆₀₀ 0.05–0.1 (0.1 is used for the plate-reader template). Culture volume to add = (target OD × final volume) ÷ starter OD. Blank the spectrophotometer with sterile medium (same batch, same Tween/supplements). Read time zero immediately after inoculating. Keep the same cuvette type throughout. Incubate at 37 °C with shaking (see the table for rates). Sample at regular intervals (table below). Mix the culture, remove about 1 mL aseptically, read OD₆₀₀. Dilute samples above OD 0.6–0.8 in medium and multiply the reading by the dilution factor, because the spectrophotometer is not linear at high density. Continue until the culture plateaus (stationary phase). For replicate curves, inoculate each flask from the same starter at the same OD and run at least three biological replicates. Suggested sampling by organism E. coli S. aureus M. smegmatis Typical doubling time ~20–30 min ~30–40 min about 3 h Sampling interval every 30–60 min every 30–60 min every 2–3 h Total length 8 h 8–10 h 24–30 h Medium LB TSB 7H9 + ADC + 0.05% Tween 80 Shaking 200–250 rpm 200–250 rpm ~200 rpm, or roller BCG and M. tuberculosis double about every 18–24 h (see Strains and growth), so sample once or twice daily over one to two weeks. Work with BSL-2 organisms in a biosafety cabinet. Calculations Doubling time from two points in exponential phase: $$t_d = \frac{(t_2 - t_1)\,\ln 2}{\ln(\mathrm{OD}_2/\mathrm{OD}_1)}$$ Better: plot ln(OD) against time and fit a line through the exponential portion. Growth rate μ = slope; doubling time = ln 2 ÷ μ. Tips Plot on a log scale: exponential growth is then a straight line. Keep the flask:medium ratio and shaking speed the same between strains; aeration changes growth rate. Mycobacteria clump. Pipette the culture up and down (or vortex briefly with beads) before reading, and keep Tween 80 in the medium so that OD reflects cell number. When a drug or inducer is added, record the time and OD at the addition. Correct for OD if reading in a plate reader, since the path length differs from a 1 cm cuvette. OD does not distinguish live from dead cells. Plate for CFU (Serial dilution) when viability matters. Reading intervals, flask size and shaking speed are general guidelines and should be replaced with your lab’s usual values.

Handle M. marinum at the biosafety level required by your institution. 1. Clone the flanks into p2NIL Combine 0.5 µL DpnI-treated p2NIL vector, 0.5 µL PCR upstream flank and 0.5 µL PCR downstream flank. Add 50 µL DH5α competent cells, keep on ice at least 30 min. Heat shock 45 s at 42 °C; add 200 µL LB; 1 h at 37 °C. Spin 1 min, resuspend, plate on LB + kanamycin (p2NIL is KanR). Pick 4–8 colonies into 5 mL LB + kanamycin overnight. Miniprep. Diagnostic digest (10 µL: 1 µL 10× buffer, 2 µL DNA, 0.5 µL enzyme, 6.5 µL water; 1 h at 37 °C) with an enzyme that gives at least two bands. Check on a gel. 2. Add the pGOAL cassette (PacI) Digest p2NIL clone with PacI (same 10 µL recipe). Dephosphorylate with Antarctic phosphatase (1.5 µL buffer, 1 µL enzyme; 37 °C 30 min; 80 °C 2 min). “Cut/kill” empty pGOAL with PacI (37 °C 60 min, 65 °C 20 min, hold 25 °C). Ligate: 1 µL p2NIL, 0.5 µL water, 0.5 µL ligase buffer, 2.5 µL digested pGOAL, 0.5 µL ligase; overnight at 4 °C. Transform the whole ligation into 50 µL DH5α. Plate on LB + kanamycin + X-gal (to add X-gal to existing plates: warm, add beads and ~100 µL LB, 20 µL X-gal, shake, soak in at 37 °C). Pick blue colonies (pGOAL carries lacZ), grow in LB + kanamycin, miniprep. Check with AflII + PacI: three bands expected (two near 5 and 7 kb, one near 2 kb; use your construct map for exact sizes). 3. Transform M. marinum Use ~3 µg DNA for p2NIL/pGOAL constructs (UV-treat the DNA) and ~0.5 µg for complementation plasmids (no UV). M. marinum needs more DNA than M. tuberculosis; about 1 µg is the minimum for success. Spin 500 µL competent cells (13,000 rpm, 2 min). Wash three times with glycerol buffer (80 mL water, 20 mL 50% glycerol, 500 µL 20% Tween 80). Resuspend in 500 µL, add DNA, electroporate, and immediately add to 2 mL 7H9. Recover at 32 °C. Plate the next day on KO plates (7H11 + X-gal + kanamycin + OADC) (complementation constructs on 7H11 + hygromycin as appropriate). Pick blue colonies (single crossover); grow in 3 mL 7H9. Dilute 1:20 (10 µL + 190 µL 7H9) and plate 200 µL on sucrose plates (7H11 + X-gal + sucrose + OADC). Pick white colonies (double crossover), grow in 7H9, and confirm the knockout by PCR with confirmation primers. Advice from experienced M. marinum labs: p2NIL and pGOAL are obtained from Addgene (under a material transfer agreement). The UV treatment of the DNA is critical. Without it M. marinum integrates the plasmid at the wrong site, probably because of strong mismatch repair compared with M. tuberculosis. The glycine step in preparing competent cells improves transformation. Competent cell preparation Grow a colony in 5 mL 7H9 for 3–5 days; expand to 25 mL for 24–48 h. Add 2 mL 2 M glycine; grow 24 h. Spin the whole culture 4,000 rpm, 5 min. Wash three times with the glycerol buffer above. Resuspend in 5 mL buffer; freeze 500 µL aliquots at –80 °C. Keep wild-type stocks low-passage; avoid unnecessary passaging (the strain can lose haemolytic activity). Temperatures (32 °C vs 30 °C), UV dose and plate recipes should be checked against the original protocol.

LB See Pouring LB plates for LB broth, agar and antibiotic concentrations. 7H9 (1 L) Filter sterilize. Do not autoclave. 4.7 g 7H9 powder 2 mL glycerol (2.52 g) 2.5 mL 20% Tween 80 100 mL 10X ADC (or OADC) 900 mL dH₂O Use ADC for M. smegmatis and OADC for M. tuberculosis. 10X ADC (1 L) Supplies carbon (dextrose), toxin absorption (BSA) and radical scavenging (catalase). Filter sterilize. Do not autoclave. 50 g BSA fraction V (Sigma brand) 20 g dextrose (D-glucose) 8.5 g NaCl 0.03 g catalase dH₂O to 1 L Sauton’s (1 L) A minimal medium, without ADC, for M. smegmatis and BCG. Cells grow more slowly than in 7H9, anhydrotetracycline induction may be weaker, and some strains (for example some conditional-depletion strains) may not grow in it. 0.5 g KH₂PO₄ 0.5 g MgSO₄·7H₂O 2 g citric acid 0.05 g ferric ammonium citrate 60 mL glycerol 4 g asparagine dH₂O to 1 L Adjust pH to 7.4 with 1 M NaOH. Filter sterilize (autoclaving destroys asparagine). Add 2.5 mL 20% Tween 80 to prevent clumping. Hartmans–de Bont (HdB) minimal medium (1 L) A defined medium for M. smegmatis with growth similar to 7H9, useful for starvation experiments. Follow the order below to avoid a precipitate. Add 10 mL of 100X M-stock to dH₂O. Add the nitrogen source, 2 g (NH₄)₂SO₄ (15 mM), or 0.02 g (0.15 mM) for nitrogen starvation. Add the carbon source, 2 mL glycerol (27.4 mM), or 0.8 mL (11 mM) for carbon starvation. Bring to 990 mL with dH₂O and autoclave. Add 10 mL sterile 100X P-stock (or 100X P-starve stock for phosphate starvation). For carbon starvation, add Tween 80 or tyloxapol to 0.05% (2.5 mL of a 20% sterile stock). Filter sterilize. The medium must be autoclaved and then filter sterilized, or a precipitate forms over time. 100X M-stock (100 mL): EDTA 100 mg; MgCl₂·6H₂O 1000 mg; CaCl₂·2H₂O 10 mg; Na₂MoO₄·2H₂O 2 mg; CoCl₂·6H₂O 4 mg; MnCl₂·2H₂O 10 mg; ZnSO₄·7H₂O 20 mg; FeSO₄·7H₂O 50 mg; CuSO₄·5H₂O 2 mg. 100X P-stock (100 mL): K₂HPO₄ 15.5 g; NaH₂PO₄ 8.5 g. Autoclave. 100X P-starve stock (100 mL): K₂HPO₄ 0.155 g; NaH₂PO₄ 0.085 g; MOPS 10.46 g. Adjust to pH 7.0 and autoclave.

Buffer W: 100 mM Tris pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA. Grow 10 mL M. smegmatis to late log (OD₆₀₀ 0.6–0.9). Put a conical of acetone at –20 °C. Spin 5 min at 4 °C. Resuspend the pellet in 900 µL Buffer W + 1 mM PMSF (add 100 µL of 100 mM PMSF stock per mL; the source describes this as a 1:10 ratio). Transfer to a bead-beating tube pre-filled with beads. No Tween in the lysis buffer. Bead-beat 2 min, ice 5 min, repeat for 4 rounds. Add 120 µL 1% DDM (10 mg/mL in Buffer W) for 0.1% final. Bead-beat 1 min or vortex 1 min. Spin 5 min at 16,000 rpm in the cold. Keep the supernatant; discard the pellet. Measure A₂₈₀ (NanoDrop, blank: Buffer W + PMSF). Normalize all samples to the lowest concentration and bring to 1 mL. Add 250 µL TCA (the source says “TCA”, concentration not given; commonly 100% w/v stock). Incubate 10 min on ice. Spin max speed 5 min in the cold. Remove the supernatant without disturbing the pellet. Wash with 200 µL cold acetone; spin 5 min in the cold; remove acetone. Repeat once. Evaporate the acetone (open tubes or heat briefly). Resuspend in 42 µL Buffer W + 8.3 µL 6× Laemmli. If the dye turns yellow (acidic), add 0.5 µL saturated NaOH and mix; repeat until blue and the pellet dissolves. Heat 10 min at 95 °C and run on a gel. See Western blot. TCA stock concentration not stated in the source.

Layout Use rows B–G and columns 2–11. Fill the outer wells with 200 µL sterile water to limit evaporation. Column 2: highest drug concentration, no bacteria (drug-only control). Columns 3–10: two-fold dilution series (column 3 highest). Column 11: bacteria, no drug. Plan concentrations Estimate the MIC from the literature or earlier experiments and place it in the middle of the series (column 6 or 7). Calculate two-fold steps above and below it and write the values as “actual” concentrations. Antibiotic is diluted 2-fold when cells are added, and cells 2-fold when added to drug, so prepare the drug at twice the final concentration (“preliminary” values). Set-up Use log-phase cultures (OD 0.1–0.6). Medium must support growth (7H9 or HdB complete; not a starvation medium). Dissolve the drug in DMSO or water at a high stock concentration. Make medium containing the drug at the highest preliminary concentration. Add 100 µL of this medium to column 2 and 200 µL to column 3. Add 100 µL plain medium to column 2 (this completes the drug-only control, final 200 µL) and 100 µL plain medium to columns 4–11. Serially transfer 100 µL from column 3 to 4, 4 to 5, and so on to column 10, mixing and changing tips each time. Discard 100 µL from column 10. Measure culture OD and dilute each biological replicate to OD 0.002. Use three biological replicates per strain. Add 100 µL diluted culture to columns 3–11 of a row (one replicate per row). Seal with a breathable plate seal and cover with the lid. Incubate at 37 °C for 48 h with shaking for M. smegmatis. Make 0.02% Alamar Blue: 0.8 mg resazurin in 4 mL water. Add 20 µL to every well except the water-filled edge wells. Reseal. Re-incubate 7–18 h for M. smegmatis. Blue = no growth; pink = growth. Violet wells at 24 h usually turn pink after another day and count as growth. MIC = lowest drug concentration that stays blue. Confirm incubation times and OD for slow-growing species; these values are for M. smegmatis.

Purpose Detect cells in phase or fluorescence images, curate the detections, export per-cell measurements, and plot fluorescence profiles and demographs. Getting started Open ImageJ (Fiji) and open the MicrobeJ plugin. For hyperstacks, go to the Images tab and switch to Folder, then import your whole folder of images. Go to Bacteria and set the channel and background. Choose the options you need: exclude on edges, shape descriptors, segmentation, intensity, shape, profile and polarity (for poles and sides, choose intensity > channel > max). Set the threshold. The example threshold used was −116; this depends on the images. To show stained colors, use ImageJ Image > Color > Arrange Channels and assign colors (for example channel 1 = GFP green, channel 2 = DAPI blue). In the Maxima tab, tick the box to edit. Choose the channel and background, change the tolerance, and choose options (exclude on edges, shape descriptors, segmentation, intensity, profile) and associations (inside, location, localization). Run the current settings on the active image to check they are appropriate. If they are, click the pencil icon at the bottom right to detect cells and load the manual editing interface. Set detection parameters Set the ranges that define a cell. The values below were used for M. smegmatis; choose ranges appropriate to your organism and magnification. Area: 1–8 Length: 0.5–10 Width: 0.2–2 (Units are not stated in the original notes; confirm they are µm² and µm.) For fluorescence images, tick the box next to polarity and set the options as in your analysis template. Choose the correct channel for the signal you are measuring (for example, the HADA channel). The channel number changes between experiments. Detect, curate and save Use the blue arrow to test your parameters on the image. Once they are good, use the pencil to generate the list of cells. In the experiment editor list, remove bad detections and cut touching cells apart. When all good cells are highlighted green, click save in the experiment editor. The experiment file should go in the experiment folder with the same name as the image file. In the experiment editor, click the graphs button (4th from the left) to open the results file. In the results file, click Bacteria to see the data for each good cell. Right-click column headings to add sub-columns. Use the same set of columns for every image. Copy the data into your spreadsheet, in a tab named for the image folder. Keep an organized system for naming and storing experiment and results files, and a consistent way of exporting to a spreadsheet. Fluorescence profile Open the results file in MicrobeJ and click Bacteria. Click the Profile icon. In Plot, choose XStat Profile; in Stat, choose mean. In Y axis, choose Medial → Intensity → the channel you measured. Click the play button. Demograph Open the results file and click Bacteria. Click the Demograph icon. In Plot, choose Profile; in Profiles, choose medial → Intensity → your channel. In Sorting, choose shape.length. Click the play button. Where it usually fails Wrong channel. Check the channel assignment before every analysis. Merged or split cells. Tighten the shape ranges and curate manually in the experiment editor. Inconsistent columns between images. Use the same set of columns for every image so exported data can be combined.

Moenomycin is a transglycosylase (PBP1-type) inhibitor. These assays combine it with anhydrotetracycline (aTc)-induced depletion of a target, so that drug sensitivity can be compared with and without depletion. See Induction and depletion systems. Kill curve (CFU) Treat cells with 100 µg/mL moenomycin and 500 ng/mL aTc. Take time points every 15 min for the first hour, then every 30 min up to 2 h. Serially dilute and plate each time point for CFU (Serial dilution and CFU). Take the zero time point before adding drug. Growth curve Treat cells with 2–3 concentrations of moenomycin (20, 50 and 100 µg/mL) and 500 ng/mL aTc, alongside no-drug and no-aTc controls. Run a plate-reader growth curve (Growth curve setup) for up to 8 h. Microscopy Add aTc first to start depletion. At each depletion time point (4, 8, 14 and 20 h): add 100 µg/mL moenomycin and roll 45 min, then add HADA and roll 15 min more at 37 °C. Wash and fix with 16% paraformaldehyde (final concentration to be confirmed). Image within 24 h of fixation. Plate, vehicle and fixation details to be confirmed by the author.

Handle phenol, chloroform and methanol in a fume hood and dispose as hazardous waste. For a fast, lower-yield and lower-purity alternative see Smash & Grab. Reagents: TE (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8, 1 mM EDTA); 1× TBS; phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1); chloroform:methanol (2:1); 1 M Tris base pH 9; lysozyme 10 mg/mL; 10% SDS; proteinase K; chloroform; chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (24:1); DNase-free RNase A; 3 M sodium acetate pH 5.2; 100% and 70% ethanol (ice-cold); 55 °C water bath or thermostat (eppendorf). Harvest 5–10 mL saturated culture, up to 60 mL log-phase culture. Optional: freeze the pellet at –80 °C for at least 4 h (weakens the cell wall; not required). Resuspend in 500 µL TE (EDTA protects DNA from nucleases). Add an equal volume of chloroform:methanol (2:1) and rock at room temperature at least 1 h. This removes cell wall lipids. Spin 2,500 × g, 20 min. The cells form a tight band at the interface. Remove the top layer; push a pipette tip through the cell layer at the side to remove the bottom layer, leaving the packed band (decanting tends to lose cells). Leave the uncapped tube at 55 °C for 10–15 min to evaporate solvent traces that inhibit lysozyme. Do not over-dry. Add 500 µL TE and vortex vigorously (the cells clump after organic extraction). Add 0.1 volume 1 M Tris base pH 9. Add 0.1 volume lysozyme stock and incubate 12–16 h at 37 °C. Do not vortex after adding lysozyme (shears DNA). Next day, place 100% ethanol at –20 °C. Loosen any chunks from the bottom of the tube with a pipette tip. Add 1 µL RNase (10 mg/mL) for ~20 µg/mL, 37 °C at least 30 min. Some RNA still co-precipitates and affects A260/280 readings. Add 0.1 volume 10% SDS and 0.01 volume proteinase K stock (the original text gives ~200 µg/mL final; check against your stock) and incubate 3 h at 55 °C, mixing by inversion. Add an equal volume of phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol. Pipette the whole mixture, not only the isoamyl alcohol layer that floats on top. Mix, spin. Move the top aqueous layer to a new tube, avoiding the white interface. Repeat 13–14 until no protein is visible at the interface (usually one more time). Add ~150 µL TE before each extraction to keep the aqueous phase at 500–700 µL. Remove residual phenol with an equal volume of chloroform; spin; keep the aqueous layer. Add 0.1 volume 3 M sodium acetate and mix. Add 2–3 volumes ice-cold 100% ethanol, mix, keep at –20 °C for 10 min to overnight. Spin at maximum speed for 10 min at 4 °C. Wash the pellet 2–3 times with ice-cold 70% ethanol. Air-dry briefly and dissolve in 50–100 µL TE.

Both protocols use hazardous reagents (chloroform, phenol, TRIzol). Work in a fume hood with appropriate protective equipment. Genomic DNA Pellet 5–10 mL of culture. Resuspend in 500 µL 2:1 chloroform:methanol and vortex for 30 s, 5 times. Add 500 µL phenol and mix. Rock at room temperature for 30 min in a sealable tube. Add 1 mL TE and rock for 1 hour at room temperature. Spin at maximum speed for 3 min and move the upper aqueous phase to a new tube. Add 1 volume isopropanol and 0.1 volume 3 M sodium acetate (pH 5.2). Mix and spin at maximum speed for 10 min at 4 °C. Wash the pellet with 200 µL 70% ethanol and pellet again for 5 min. Air-dry the pellet and resuspend in water. RNA Pellet 10 mL of culture. Add 1 mL TRIzol and bead-beat 4 times for 40 s each. Incubate at room temperature for 5 min. Add 0.2 mL chloroform and shake for 15 s. Centrifuge 15 min at 4 °C and transfer the upper aqueous phase to a new tube. Add 500 µL ice-cold isopropanol and incubate at −20 °C for 15 min. Centrifuge at maximum speed for 15 min at 4 °C and discard the supernatant. Wash the pellet in 0.7 mL 70% ethanol (made in DEPC water). Air-dry and resuspend in 100 µL DEPC water. Add 350 µL Buffer RLT and 250 µL 100% ethanol and load onto an RNeasy column. Follow the RNeasy spin instructions, stopping before the water elution. Add 10 µL DNase I to 70 µL Buffer RDD, apply to the column and digest for 1 hour at room temperature. Add 350 µL Buffer RW1, wait 5 min and centrifuge 15 s at 10,000 rpm. Wash with Buffer RPE and elute following the kit instructions. Digest the eluate again with TURBO DNase (buffer and 1 µL enzyme) at 37 °C for 30 min. Add DNase inactivation reagent (1/10 of the volume), mix and incubate at room temperature for 5 min. Centrifuge at 10,000 rpm for 5 min and transfer the RNA to a new tube for cDNA synthesis.

Materials 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes Magnetic stand for 1.5 mL tubes End-over-end rotator Pierce Anti-c-Myc Magnetic Beads (or equivalent) 1× TBS-T (25 mM Tris, 0.15 M NaCl, 0.05% Tween-20) and 5× TBS-T (125 mM Tris, 0.75 M NaCl, 0.25% Tween-20) The amount of lysate and incubation time depend on how highly the tagged protein is expressed and need optimization. For co-IP, buffers must be chosen to preserve the interaction. Mix the bead stock thoroughly before use. Procedure Place 25–100 µL beads in a tube. Add 175 µL 1× TBS-T and mix. Collect beads on the magnet; discard supernatant. Wash with 1 mL 1× TBS-T (invert or gently vortex 1 min). Collect and discard supernatant. Add the sample (about 100 µg protein in 100 µL) and 400 µL 1× TBS-T. Incubate 30 min at room temperature with mixing. Collect the beads. Save the unbound fraction for analysis. Wash three times with 300 µL 5× TBS-T. Wash once with 300 µL ultrapure water. Elution (choose one) Gentle (peptide): 100 µL c-Myc peptide at 0.5 mg/mL in TBS, 37 °C for 5–10 min on a rotator (lower temperature gives lower yield). Repeat once for better recovery. Use this if the protein must stay functional or is pH-sensitive. Basic: 100 µL 50 mM NaOH, 5 min at room temperature; neutralize with 50 µL neutralization buffer per 100 µL eluate. Acidic: 100 µL IgG elution buffer (pH 2.0) or 0.1 M glycine pH 2.0, 5–10 min at room temperature; neutralize with 15 µL neutralization buffer per 100 µL eluate. SDS sample buffer: 100 µL, 95–100 °C for 5–10 min. Non-reducing buffer reduces interference from co-eluting antibody fragments. For reducing conditions add 2.5 µL 2 M DTT per 100 µL. Always include a negative control (beads with lysate from untagged cells) and keep the unbound fraction and washes for blotting.

For conjugation from an E. coli donor, see bi-parental conjugation. Filter mating Inoculate TSB or 7H9 broth (with Tween 80) containing the appropriate antibiotic with each strain to be mated. Incubate at 250 rpm and 37 °C overnight. By 18–24 hours the cultures should be near the end of log phase, with A₆₀₀ around 1.5. Place 0.5 mL each of donor and recipient into a microcentrifuge tube and pellet for 30 s. Resuspend in 1 mL TSB without Tween and pellet for 30 s. Wash once more. Resuspend the cells in 100 µL TSB.
