Gently spot the whole 100 µL onto the center of a 0.45 µm membrane filter (it need not be sterile) placed on a pre-warmed TSA plate. Four or five filters fit on one plate if labeled carefully. Incubate the plate right side up for 18–24 h at 30 °C. Remove the filter with sterile forceps into a sterile tube. Rinse the cells off with 1 mL TSB + Tween using a pipette, and vortex for 15–30 s. Mycobacteria clump and are hard to resuspend after growth on solid medium; pipetting up and down with a tip helps make the suspension uniform. Dilute and plate on selective agar: Dilute to 10⁻⁶ and 10⁻⁷ and plate 0.1 mL of the appropriate dilutions on plates with a single antibiotic selecting for either the donor or the recipient. Plate 0.1 mL of the original suspension and of the 10⁻¹ and 10⁻² dilutions on plates containing both antibiotics, to select transconjugants that carry both resistance genes. Adjust the dilutions to the growth of the strains. Incubate at 37 °C. Colonies are visible after 2–3 days and countable from 3–4 days. Mini-mating (qualitative) Generates transconjugants but not quantitative data. Mix 50 µL each of recipient and donor with 1 mL TSB without Tween. Spin for 30 s. Wash with 1 mL and spin for 30 s. Resuspend the pellet in 25 µL broth and spot onto a TSA plate without antibiotics. Incubate at 30 °C for 18–24 h. Collect the spot with a sterile loop and resuspend in 200 µL TSB with 0.05% Tween 80, mixing with a pipette tip. Spread on the appropriate antibiotic plates (for example kanamycin + streptomycin): 20 µL on one plate and the remaining 180 µL on another. Incubate at the proper temperature. Alternative wash: put 1 mL TSB (no Tween) in a microcentrifuge tube, add 50 µL each of recipient and donor, spin 30 s, tip off the supernatant, add 1 mL TSB and mix, spin 30 s, and tip off all but the last drop (about 25 µL). Then continue from step 2 above, resuspending in the remaining 25 µL. Microtiter-plate matings (for screens) Use fresh colonies (less than a week old); otherwise transfer efficiencies fall. Day 1. Add 200 µL TSB with appropriate antibiotic to the wells of a microtiter dish using a multichannel pipettor and sterile troughs. In column 1 (rows A–G), include controls: 4 wells of broth only and 4 wells of wild-type donor. Inoculate columns 2–12 (rows A–G) with donor colonies for the screen. Cover with an air-permeable tape sheet and incubate with gentle shaking for 48 h at 37 °C. (The 48 h could probably be reduced with deeper wells that can be shaken more vigorously.) Day 2. Grow 20 mL of the recipient strain (streptomycin resistant). Each well needs 200 µL, so 1 plate needs about 20 mL. A single large flask is fine. Day 3. Add 50 µL TSB with Tween to a new microtiter dish and use a replicator to inoculate wells from the donor plate for glycerol stocks. Grow overnight with gentle shaking at 37 °C. Alternatively, transfer 20 µL into a new dish with 20 µL of 30% glycerol and freeze immediately. Spin the remaining cells at 2700 rpm for 3 min in a benchtop centrifuge and dump the supernatant by inverting the dish. Resuspend cells in 200 µL of recipient culture. Controls: add recipient to two wild-type donor wells (donor + recipient, positive control) and to two broth-only wells. Column 1 then contains donor + recipient, donor only, recipient only and broth only. Spin down and dump the supernatant. Wash twice with TSB without Tween. After the second wash, resuspend in 10 µL TSB without Tween. Spot 5 µL onto a large TSA microtiter dish and incubate colony side up for 48 h at 30 °C. Day 4. Add another 50 µL TSB + 30% glycerol to the glycerol dish growing at 37 °C and freeze at −70 °C. Day 5. Replica-plate the mating plate with velvet onto TSA + antibiotic + streptomycin (to select transconjugants) and onto TSA + antibiotic (to select donor). Invert and incubate at 37 °C for 4 days. After 4–5 days you will see speckled growth of transconjugants for each spot, generally 20–50 small colonies per spot. Low frequencies generally mean the inoculum was not from fresh colonies. Streak positive culture wells onto the appropriate antibiotic plates. Repeat the screen using 4 individual colonies from the streak-out. The microtiter format allows independent positives to be screened in parallel. If cultures are still positive, perform a filter mating to determine the transfer frequency accurately compared to a control. Freeze each clone as a glycerol stock. Careful labeling and tracking of microtiter dishes and clones is essential. Keep a spreadsheet for each dish, photograph each mating plate screen, and track clones by plate, well and date. Volumes were given as “ml” in the source where microliters are clearly meant; they have been read as µL.

Workflow Clone the gene into a vector with a His tag (e.g. pET28 or pET21). Transform an expression strain: BL21 if the gene has no codon bias; BL21 Codon Plus if it has a GC-rich codon bias; a cold-adapted chaperone strain (e.g. Arctic Express Codon Plus) if the protein is still insoluble in BL21 Codon Plus. Test induction (Test inductions): pre-induction, post-induction, supernatant and pellet samples on a gel. Adjust conditions until most of the protein is soluble. Ni column: large-scale expression (~1 L), lysis, and loading of the supernatant on a Ni column in low-imidazole buffer. Wash with low-imidazole buffer; elute with high imidazole. Check fractions on a gel. See His-SUMO purification for a worked example. Size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) to separate folded from aggregated or unfolded protein; check fractions on a gel. Concentrate, aliquot and snap-freeze in liquid nitrogen. Practical notes EDTA and Ni columns. EDTA chelates Ni²⁺ and reduces binding, so leave EDTA out of the wash and elution buffers (a low level in the lysis buffer can stabilize some proteins). If a protein precipitates without EDTA after the column, add it back at the dialysis/SEC stage. Filter and degas buffers for FPLC; filter (0.45 µm) or spin lysates twice before loading. Bubbles damage columns. Prime lines whenever you change buffers and set pressure limits for every run. Keep both pump lines in liquid. Store columns in 20% ethanol and flush with water before switching to salt buffers. Packing an empty cartridge with Ni-NTA resin (Example: 5 mL empty Bio-Scale Mini cartridges, Bio-Rad.) Assemble the cartridge. Pour up to 5 mL Ni-NTA resin into the inner cartridge. Draw the liquid through with a peristaltic pump (as vacuum at the bottom) or a vacuum. Add more resin and repeat until the cartridge is full and tightly packed. Slide the outer cartridge over the packed inner cartridge, fit the ring, and invert it to connect to the chromatography system. Connect “water to water”: run ethanol/water at 2 mL/min, connect the top of the cartridge to the system at the column position (fluid should be dripping from the connector), then connect the bottom. The outlet should be flowing before you connect the bottom. See the manufacturer’s manual for your column and instrument.

The method for pKM402 (Ptet-RecT)-promoted oligo recombineering in M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis follows the same procedures as dsDNA recombineering for growing and preparing cells for electroporation, with the exceptions below. Differences from dsDNA recombineering Induce the culture with 50 ng/mL anhydrotetracycline (aTc), starting at OD₆₀₀ = 0.5, for 3 hours. Electroporate about 1 µg of oligo. Resuspend the electroporated cells in 10 mL 7H9 and grow out at 37 °C for 4–7 days (M. tuberculosis) or overnight (M. smegmatis). If there is more than one chromosome copy per cell at electroporation and only one is modified, the culture must be grown out so the modified chromosome segregates. For M. tuberculosis about a week is used. Plate on selective medium that you expect to select for the mutation. If you cannot select for your mutation, use the co-transformation strategy below. Oligo substrate The oligo should be 70 bases, with the mutation(s) in the middle. Order the oligo that targets the lagging-strand template of the replication fork. Because this is often hard to know, order both the top strand and the bottom strand (each with the change). In most cases one works much better than the other (the lagging-strand oligo); the other often does not work at all, like the no-DNA control. Resuspend the oligo to 0.5 µg/µL in 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0. Add 2 µL oligo (1 µg) to 400 µL of electrocompetent M. smegmatis carrying pKM402. Control oligo This oligo makes a 1 bp change in the rpsL locus and confers streptomycin resistance. It is specific to M. smegmatis; a different oligo is needed for M. tuberculosis. CGCGCGCGACCTTCCGGAGGGCCGAGTTCGGCTTCCTCGGAGTGGTGGTGTAAACGCGCGTGCACACGCC Plate 200 µL of undiluted, 10⁻¹ and 10⁻² dilutions on plates containing 20 µg/mL streptomycin after overnight growth (M. smegmatis) or one week (M. tuberculosis). Plate 200 µL of the 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁶ dilutions for a total cell count. Expect about 10⁴–10⁵ recombinants per 10⁸ total cells for rpsL (the change you want may or may not be in this range). Also do a no-DNA control. Co-transformation with the rpsL oligo (when you cannot select for your mutation) Co-transform the oligo that makes your mutation together with the rpsL oligo and select on streptomycin. Then screen the streptomycin-resistant colonies for your mutation by MAMA-PCR. The idea is that a cell that took up and recombined one oligo is more likely than a random cell to have done so with a second. Transform 1 µg of each oligo into the pKM402 strain as above and select on plates with streptomycin. Make a plasmid or PCR product containing your desired point mutation (for example by stitch PCR, with the mutation in the middle of the primers). This is needed to optimize the MAMA-PCR. Also have a wild-type version ready. Design primers for MAMA-PCR (mismatch amplification mutation assay): primer F upstream of the mutation, primer mutR whose very 3′ end matches only the mutant sequence (a single 3′ mismatch is fine), and primer R downstream of the mutation as a control for the reaction and template. Primer F + mutR Primer F + R Mutant DNA product product Wild-type DNA no product product Optimize the MAMA-PCR by gradient PCR using mutant and wild-type DNA, finding an annealing temperature at which F + mutR gives product only on mutant template. Pick 96 streptomycin-resistant colonies into a 96-well PCR plate with 10 µL DMSO per well, and patch the colonies on an agar plate. Boil at 95 °C for 1 hour. Pool 12 samples at a time, giving 8 pooled samples per plate. Run MAMA-PCR on the pools, replacing the DMSO in the PCR mix with DMSO from the samples. Choose one or two pools giving a product with F + mutR and repeat un-pooled. Depending on the target, expect about 5–20% of streptomycin-resistant colonies to carry the second mutation. Sequence PCR-positive mutants. Sequence the PCR product from primers F and R, not mutR. The source gives streptomycin as “20 mg/mL”; this is read as 20 µg/mL.

Overview An oligo containing the Bxb1 attP site flanked by 70 bases of target sequence is recombined into the chromosome, and a payload plasmid is then integrated at the attP site by Bxb1 integrase. Organism: the conditions (37 °C, 3 days) suggest M. smegmatis; confirm. Steps Design and order the oligo. Include the Bxb1 attP site (GGTTTGTCTGGTCAACCACCGCGGTCTCAGTGGTGTACGGTACAAACC, 48 nt) flanked by 70 bases of target sequence on each side. For a C-terminal tag, insert attP between the last codon and the stop codon: copy the sequence from 70 bases upstream of the insertion point to 70 bases downstream. Decide whether the oligo is the top strand or its reverse complement (see the oligo-directionality guidance for ORBIT). Order the 188 nt oligo as an Ultramer. Prepare the payload vector. Miniprep the appropriate ORBIT vector. Grow the recipient strain. The strain carrying the inducible recombinase and integrase plasmid is grown in 7H9 + kanamycin: 10 mL per transformation, grown to turbidity. The night before, do a calculated dilution so that the culture is at OD about 0.5 the next morning. Induce. In the morning, measure the OD and adjust to 0.5. Induce the integrase with 500 ng/mL anhydrotetracycline (aTc) and shake or roll for 3 hours. Make competent cells. Wash the induced cells three times in ice-cold 10% glycerol. Cool the centrifuge, pellet the cells at 4000 rpm for 5 min, resuspend in 10 mL cold 10% glycerol, repeat twice, then pellet once more and resuspend in 500 µL cold 10% glycerol for a single transformation. Prepare cuvettes while spinning. For one transformation you need two cuvettes, the transformation and a control with no oligo. Control: pipette 0.4 µg of the ORBIT vector onto the side of the cuvette. Transformation: pipette 0.4 µg of ORBIT vector and 1 µg of oligo. Pipette 250 µL of the washed competent cells into each cuvette and tap to remove bubbles. Electroporate at 2500 V, 1000 Ω, 25 µF after drying each cuvette. The time constant should be about 20 ms. Transfer the cells into labeled tubes with 1 mL 7H9, tape them to a roller and roll at 37 °C for 3 hours. Have at least two LB + hygromycin 50 µg/mL plates ready. Spin the tubes for 1 min at maximum speed. Resuspend in 150 µL 7H9. Put beads on the plates, add the 150 µL of cells and spread. Incubate at 37 °C for 3 days. PCR check each junction: for the left flank, use an oriE reverse primer with a target-specific forward primer; for the right flank, use a hygromycin-cassette forward primer with a target-specific reverse primer. Which strand to order (oligo directionality) Which strand you order depends on both the position and the direction of the gene on the chromosome. The underlying reason (annealing to the lagging-strand template) is general knowledge, not from the source note; confirm. Take the gene sequence in the 5′→3′ coding orientation (the “top” strand in a sequence file; databases such as Tuberculist always give the gene reading 5′→3′ regardless of orientation on the chromosome). Its reverse complement is the “bottom” strand. Insert the attP site into the sequence before choosing the strand (not critical for deletions, critical for fusions). Find the replicore: M. smegmatis: right replicore ~0–3.4 Mb, left replicore ~3.5–6.9 Mb (the note gives 0–3.3 and 3.3–6.4 Mb in places; confirm) M. tuberculosis: right replicore 0–2.2 Mb, left replicore 2.3–4.4 Mb Rule of thumb: if the gene reads toward the origin, order the sequence as it appears in your file (top strand). If it reads away from the origin, order the reverse complement. Replicore Gene reads Order Right toward origin (counterclockwise) top strand (as in file) Right away from origin (clockwise) reverse complement Left away from origin (counterclockwise) reverse complement Left toward origin (clockwise) top strand (as in file) Source and author of this directionality note are not recorded in the file; add credit if known. Replicore boundaries differ between the paragraphs in the original.

Primer stocks below are 10 µM. Taq-based master mix (GoTaq): checking colonies and lysates Low fidelity. Do not use for cloning. Supplied as a 2X mix containing nucleotides, salts, enzyme and loading dye. See also colony PCR. 10 µL reaction: 5 µL master mix, 0.5 µL forward primer, 0.5 µL reverse primer, 0.5 µL DMSO, 3.5 µL water (minus template volume). KOD Xtreme: high-fidelity, GC-rich cloning Extension at 68 °C, not 72 °C, at about 1 min/kb. 50 µL reaction: 0.5 µL KOD Xtreme, 1.5 µL forward primer, 1.5 µL reverse primer, 2.5 µL DMSO, 10 µL KOD Xtreme dNTPs, 25 µL 2X KOD Xtreme buffer, water, and template. The listed components add to 41 µL plus 7.5 µL water minus template, which is 48.5 µL before template; water plus template should total 9 µL to reach 50 µL. Q5: high fidelity, AT- or GC-rich templates 50 µL reaction: 1 µL template, 2.5 µL each primer, 1 µL dNTPs (10 mM each), 10 µL Q5 reaction buffer, 10 µL Q5 GC enhancer, 0.5 µL Q5 polymerase, and water to 50 µL (22.5 µL with these amounts). A cycling program is given in the Gibson assembly protocol. Phusion: high fidelity and processivity Not well optimized for GC-rich DNA. Extension about 15 s/kb. There are two buffers: HF (higher fidelity) and GC (lower fidelity, for GC-rich organisms). 10:1 Taq:Pfu mix Balances the flexibility of Taq with some proofreading by Pfu. Use when Phusion has failed, especially in stitching reactions. Where it usually fails When a PCR fails, the usual cause is an annealing temperature that does not suit the primers. The first thing to try is a gradient PCR across 50–70 °C (see Gibson assembly).

A. Isolate peptidoglycan (PG) from E. coli Grow 500 mL E. coli in LB at 37 °C to OD₆₀₀ 0.6–0.8. Chill on ice 10 min. Pellet at 4,000 × g, 15 min, 4 °C. Resuspend in 20 mL PBS (pH 7.4). Add dropwise to 80 mL boiling 5% SDS and boil 30 min with vigorous stirring. Cool to room temperature (not on ice; SDS precipitates). Optional: leave overnight at room temperature. Pellet and wash: Ultracentrifuge: 100,000 × g, 1 h, 25 °C. Wash 3× with water, 1 h spin each. Floor centrifuge: 14,000 rpm, 1 h, 25 °C. Wash at least 6× with 50 mL water. Resuspend in 1 mL PBS with α-chymotrypsin (100 µL of 3 mg/mL in 50% glycerol; Sigma C3142) to remove cell-wall-attached protein. Shake at 37 °C overnight, add another 100 µL, and incubate 3–4 h more. Add 1% SDS and incubate 1–2 h at 95 °C. Cool to room temperature. Pellet (14,000 rpm, 25 °C, 1 h) and wash at least 4× with 25 mL water to remove SDS. A 1 mL wash was also noted as a possible alternative; not confirmed. Resuspend purified PG in 500 µL 0.02% sodium azide (Sigma S2002). Stable at 4 °C for up to about 1 month. B. Purify the His-tagged protein (example: His-SBD) Express in E. coli BL21 and purify following your standard His-tag protocol (see Test inductions and His-SUMO purification). Buffer: 50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 20 mM imidazole (wash) / 250 mM imidazole (elution). Induction: 5–6 h at 25 °C, 220 rpm. Size on gel for the example construct: 19.3 kDa (with TM) and 17.3 kDa (without TM). C. Binding assay Mix 100 µg PG with 10 µg protein in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8, 500 mM NaCl, final volume 125 µL. Incubate 30 min at 4 °C with agitation. Spin 10 min at 15,000 × g. Keep the supernatant (unbound/soluble). Add 6× Laemmli and heat 10 min at 95 °C. Wash the pellet twice with 250 µL buffer, resuspend in 100 µL buffer (bound/insoluble fraction). Analyze soluble and insoluble fractions by SDS-PAGE. Include a no-PG control (protein alone) so that any sedimentation of the protein by itself is seen.

For the general method see Test inductions for protein expression. This page is the worksheet-style version for two expression temperatures. Day 1 Grow a 5 mL starter of the expression strain with the plasmid antibiotics (example: chloramphenicol 25 µg/mL + ampicillin 140 µg/mL). Record the OD. Add 2.5 mL starter to each of two flasks (A, B) of 50 mL LB + ampicillin. Grow at 37 °C to OD₆₀₀ 0.6. Always grow at 37 °C before adding IPTG, then move to the induction temperature. Record pre-induction OD for A and B. Save a pre-induction sample: 500 µL culture + 100 µL 6× Laemmli (Pre-A, Pre-B). Add 1 mM IPTG to both. Express flask A at 25 °C and flask B at 18 °C for ~16 h. Day 2 Read the OD of A and B. To load equal cell equivalents, compute X = OD(post) ÷ OD(pre), then take 500/X µL of culture and make up to 500 µL with water (500 − 500/X µL). Example: post 6, pre 0.6 → X = 10 → 50 µL culture + 450 µL water. Store as Post-A / Post-B in 100 µL 6× Laemmli. Heat 95 °C, 10 min. Pellet the cultures and freeze at –20 °C. Gel: 20 µL each of pre-A, post-A, pre-B, post-B. Lysis of the pellets Resuspend each pellet in 30 mL buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 20% glycerol). Add 300 µL 100 mM PMSF and a pinch of lysozyme; 30 min on ice. Sonicate (power 4, 10 pulses of 30 s, 10 s rests). Centrifuge 40 min at 12,000 rpm. Move supernatants to new tubes (sup-25 °C, sup-18 °C). Mix 500 µL supernatant with 100 µL 6× Laemmli (Sup-A, Sup-B). Resuspend each pellet in 30 mL buffer; mix 500 µL with 100 µL 6× Laemmli (Pellet-A, Pellet-B). Heat all samples 90–95 °C for 10 min. Run on a gel to compare soluble and insoluble fractions at each temperature.

Idea Immobilize a His-SUMO “bait” (e.g. His-SUMO-MurJ ICD) on resin. Pass the untagged “prey” (e.g. CwlM, phosphorylated by PknB or not) over it. Prey that is retained in the elution but not on a bait-free control column interacts with the bait. Use cobalt resin for the kinase/ULP stage and a 20 mM imidazole wash with no elution buffer when you want only to remove uncleaved tagged protein; use nickel for the pull-down. Part 1: Kinase and protease reactions Thaw His-SUMO-CwlM and PknB. NanoDrop with the kinase buffer as blank. Example: CwlM 0.48 mg/mL; PknB 1.80 mg/mL. Use a 1:10 kinase:substrate mass ratio. Example: 144 µg CwlM in 300 µL needs 14 µg PknB (7.8 µL). Set up two tubes, CwlM~P (phosphorylated) and NPC (no-phosphorylation control): 300 µL CwlM each, PknB in both, MnCl₂ to 1 mM from a 25 mM stock (14 µL in 350 µL), and 0.5 mM ATP (7 µL from 25 mM) only in CwlM~P. Keep ATP at –80 °C until needed. Incubate 40 min at 25 °C. Meanwhile prepare Ni (or cobalt) columns: place a frit at the bottom using a pipette tip, add 500 µL resin slurry (bed ~250 µL), drain, wash with a column of nanopure water, then 3 CV of 20 mM-imidazole wash buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 350 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, 10% glycerol), pipetting on the side. Add ULP (SUMO protease) at 1:10 by mass (e.g. 14.4 µg, 16 µL of 0.968 mg/mL) plus 34 µL 10× protease buffer to each tube (400 µL final) after the 40 min kinase step. Incubate time and temperature to be added. Load each reaction onto its column. Collect flow-through; wash twice with 250 µL wash buffer; elute with 250 µL elution buffer (same as wash but with 250 mM imidazole). Cleaved CwlM is in the flow-through and first wash; the tag and uncleaved protein stay on the resin. Run 25 µL of each fraction + 5 µL warmed 6× Laemmli (95 °C) on a gel (10 µL per lane) with PknB, ULP and the kinase reaction. Pool the flow-through and wash 1 once the gel confirms cleavage. NanoDrop. High imidazole can distort readings; if so assume ~90% yield of the cleavage reaction. Clean columns: run elution buffer, then water twice, then 20% ethanol (half through); close the column, shake, and pour the resin into a labeled “used resin” container at 4 °C. Do not discard resin. Part 2: Interaction assay (gravity columns) Four small columns: NPC experiment, NPC control, CwlM~P experiment, CwlM~P control. Each prey sample is split in two (one bait, one no-bait control). Thaw His-SUMO-MurJ ICD (example 1.082 mg/mL); use a 1:1 molar/mass ratio with the prey in the column. Prepare 250 µL-bed columns, wash with 750 µL water and 750 µL 20 mM imidazole wash buffer. Control column: load 250 µL wash buffer (tube A). Experimental column: load bait in wash buffer (tube 1). Wash with 250 µL wash buffer twice (tubes 2 and 3). Load 250 µL prey (CwlM~P or NPC) (tube 4). Elute with 500 µL elution buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.4, 350 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 250 mM imidazole) (tube 5). Mix 50 µL of each fraction with 10 µL pre-warmed 6× Laemmli, heat 95 °C for 10 min, run on a gel. Fractions: flow-through, wash 1, prey load, wash 2, elution. Part 2 (alternative): Magnetic beads Pipette 40 µL HisPur Ni-NTA magnetic beads into a tube, add 160 µL wash buffer, vortex 10 s, collect beads on a magnetic stand, discard supernatant. Wash once more in 400 µL. Bait: dilute His-SUMO bait to 400 µL in SEC buffer (aim for 1:1 with the prey: e.g. if 190 µg prey is recovered, use 95 µg bait), add to the beads, vortex, and keep on ice for ~15 min with gentle flicking every 5 min. Collect beads; save the supernatant (fraction 1, flow-through). Wash with 400 µL wash buffer (fraction 2). Add the prey (flow-through and washes from the cobalt step, ~710 µL diluted to 800 µL; split between control and experiment, 400 µL each). Mix, incubate with periodic mixing for 15 min. Save the supernatant (fraction 3). Wash with 400 µL wash buffer (fraction 4). Resuspend beads in 400 µL buffer, add 80 µL 6× Laemmli, heat 95 °C for 10 min (fraction 5, elution). Run all fractions on a gel. Some volumes and incubation times were left blank in the source drafts. They are marked above and need to be filled in from lab notes.

Radioactivity: work only in an approved radioisotope area with training and monitoring. See also In vitro kinase assay. Planning Take 10 or 20 µL samples before and after ATP at several time points. You may need to load the same kinase-reaction sample (0 min, no PstP) more than once on a gel, so calculate how much substrate and total kinase-reaction volume you need to cover every sample and control. Use kinase:substrate at 1:10 (w/w). (5:1 substrate:kinase was used for Wag31.) Kinase step (examples) Substrate Kinase Conditions His-SUMO-CwlM His-MBP-PknB 30 min, room temperature, 0.15 µCi/µL [γ-³²P]ATP, 2 mM MnCl₂, kinase buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 250 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) His-FhaA His-MBP-PknB 45 min at 37 °C, 0.15 µCi/µL [γ-³²P]ATP, 5 mM MnCl₂, 25 mM Tris pH 7.5, 1 mM DTT His-Wag31 His-MBP-PknA 2 h, room temperature, 0.2 µCi/µL [γ-³²P]ATP, 10 mM MnCl₂, 50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 20% glycerol, 150 mM NaCl Take a sample at the end of the kinase step (0 min, no PstP). Split the remainder equally into tubes: one for a no-phosphatase control (phosphatase buffer only) and one for each PstP variant (and each independently purified batch). Phosphatase step Add PstP (catalytic domain; wild-type or phosphomimetic variants) at one-tenth the mass of substrate, in phosphatase buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 10 mM MnCl₂, 1 mM DTT). Incubate at room temperature and take samples into 6× Laemmli: CwlM: 1, 3, 5, 10, 20 and 40 min FhaA: 5, 10, 20, 40, 60 and 80 min Wag31: 15, 30, 45, 60, 90 and 120 s Use two independently purified batches of each PstP variant as biological replicates. Gel Heat samples 95 °C for 10 min, then load equal amounts of substrate in each lane. Calculate substrate per µL carefully for this. Run, dry and image as for the kinase assay.

Buffers and media LB (1 L): 10 g tryptone, 10 g NaCl, 5 g yeast extract. For plates add 20 g agar. Autoclave; add antibiotic after the medium cools. Φ broth (500 mL): 10 g tryptone (2%), 2.5 g yeast extract (0.5%), 2.5 g MgSO₄ (listed as 0.4%), 0.37 g KCl (10 mM). Autoclave. TJB1 (250 mL): 3.0 g RbCl (100 mM), 2.47 g MnCl₂·4H₂O (50 mM), 0.74 g potassium acetate (30 mM), 0.36 g CaCl₂·2H₂O (10 mM), 37.5 mL glycerol (15%) or 75 mL of 50% glycerol. Adjust to pH 5.8 with HCl, slowly and without overshooting; adding NaOH to correct will precipitate salts. Filter sterilize and store at 4 °C. TJB2 (100 mL): 1.10 g CaCl₂·2H₂O (75 mM), 0.20 g MOPS (10 mM), 0.12 g RbCl (10 mM), 15 mL glycerol (15%) or 30 mL of 50% glycerol. Adjust to pH 7.0 with NaOH. Filter sterilize and store at 4 °C. Preparing the cells Day 1. Grow 5 mL of the strain overnight in LB. Day 2. Inoculate 1 mL of the overnight culture into each of 2 flasks containing 100 mL Φ broth. Shake at 30 °C until OD₆₀₀ reaches 0.50 (2–3 hours). Chill the cultures on ice for 10 min. Transfer to four 50 mL conical tubes. Centrifuge at 4 °C, 3000 rpm (1900 × g), for 5 min and discard the supernatant. Resuspend each pellet in 15 mL ice-cold TJB1 (shaking the tubes works well). Chill on ice for 5 min. Centrifuge at 4 °C, 3000 rpm (1900 × g), for 5 min and discard the supernatant. Resuspend each pellet in 2 mL ice-cold TJB2. Snap-freeze 100 µL (or 50 µL) aliquots in liquid nitrogen. Do not use ethanol–dry ice. Store at −80 °C. Transformation Thaw one tube of cells per transformation on ice and resuspend by gently tapping the tube. Add DNA and mix by swirling the pipette tip. Do not pipette up and down. Incubate on ice for 20 min. Heat shock in a 42 °C water bath for 45 s. Return to ice for 2 min. Add 200 µL SOC (or LB) and shake at 37 °C for 45 min. Plate the entire contents of the tube on LB agar with the appropriate antibiotic.

Other recombineering protocols on this site differ from this one, including in the inducer, induction timing and cell handling: an alternative M. smegmatis protocol, oligo-mediated recombineering and ORBIT. They have not been reconciled with this page. Homologous recombination (suicide plasmid) Used for insertional crosses and clean knockouts. Requires at least 1 µg of suicide plasmid per transformation and at least 500 bp of identical sequence between plasmid and target. Yield is usually fewer than 10 colonies per transformation, so do multiple transformations. Single insertion: clone about 500 bp of the target gene into a suicide plasmid. Clean knockout: clone about 1 kb upstream and 1 kb downstream of the target gene into pJM1 or another sacB-containing vector. Transform the suicide vector into M. smegmatis and select on the appropriate antibiotic. Grow cells without antibiotic to allow the second recombination event. Select for loss of sacB on 10% sucrose. Ideally about 50% of the survivors are knockouts. Recombineering (RecE/RecT) Uses mycobacteriophage RecE and RecT homologues, in a lambda-Red-like system. Flank an antibiotic cassette with about 500 bp of sequence upstream and downstream of the target gene. Two cassettes with lox sites on both sides are available. Generate the linear fragment by stitch PCR or Gibson; you need about 1 µg per transformation. Grow cells carrying the RecE/RecT plasmid (see vector guide). Induce overnight with IVN (light sensitive) at a 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸ dilution of the stock to mid-log phase (OD 0.4–0.6). The induction section gives 10⁻⁶–10⁻⁷; confirm. Make competent cells as usual (protocol) but resuspend at 1/20 of the usual final volume, and use 400 µL per transformation. Transform about 1000 ng of linear DNA. Settings: 2500 V, 1000 Ω, 25 µF. The time constant should be 20–30 ms. Outgrow for 2–3 hours in 7H9. If knocking out an essential gene, include aTc when a tet-inducible second copy is at the L5 site. Select on the appropriate antibiotic (usually fewer than 10 colonies per transformation).

Not the preferred approach: Gibson assembly is easier and usually better. Digest 1 µg of vector and the PCR product. Gel-purify the vector backbone (gel purification). The PCR product can be column-purified. Elute in 30 µL water for higher yields. Ligate with fresh T4 ligase buffer at a 3:1 insert:vector molar ratio. Ng insert = 3 × (kb insert) ÷ (kb vector) × 50 ng vector. Ligate in 10 µL with 0.5 µL T4 ligase, overnight at 16 °C or 3 hours at room temperature. For electroporation, dialyze the whole ligation on a membrane over water for 30 min (not needed for chemically competent cells). Thaw E. coli competent cells on ice for 15 min. Electroporate the entire dialyzed ligation in a cold cuvette, or add the ligation to chemically competent cells and heat shock for 1 min. Recover electroporated cells in 1 mL LB at 37 °C for 1 hour. Spin at maximum speed for 30 s, pour off the LB, resuspend in the remaining liquid and streak onto a prewarmed plate.

Work in an RNase-free area. Wipe benches, pipettes and gloves with an RNase-decontaminating wipe. Have everything ready first and move quickly. Harvest Cool a centrifuge to 4 °C. Use 20–30 mL culture at OD ~0.5–1 per biological replicate. Note RNA yield against starting OD the first time you do this. Optional RNAlater (to freeze the transcriptome and process many samples together; steps unverified in the source): add an equal volume of RNAlater, mix, wait a few minutes at room temperature, then add water or PBS equal to ¼ of the current volume so the cells pellet. Store at 4 °C short-term or –20 °C for up to a month. Without RNAlater: chill cultures on ice. Spin 4,000 rpm, 10 min, 4 °C (20 °C if RNAlater was used). Remove all supernatant; with RNAlater it is essential to remove all of it. If the pellet is disturbed, re-spin. Lysis Resuspend the pellet in 750 µL TRIzol and transfer to a bead-beating tube. Bead-beat 45 s, rest 5 min at room temperature (TRIzol stabilizes the sample); bead-beat 30 s, rest 5 min. Spin 15,000 rpm for 1 min. Purification (Direct-zol RNA kit; follow the kit manual) All at room temperature, spins 30 s at 10,000–16,000 × g. Move the supernatant to an RNase-free 2 mL tube. Add an equal volume of 95–100% ethanol and mix. Load 700 µL at a time on a column; spin; discard flow-through. On-column DNase (kit DNase): wash with 400 µL RNA wash buffer; add 5 µL DNase I + 75 µL digestion buffer; 15 min at room temperature. (Skip if using DNase Turbo afterwards.) Wash twice with 400 µL Direct-zol PreWash. Wash with 700 µL RNA wash buffer, 2 min spin, twice. Elute with 100 µL DNase/RNase-free water. Keep RNA on ice if used the same day, –20 °C for days, –80 °C for weeks. Avoid freeze-thaw cycles. Quality and DNase treatment NanoDrop with kit water as blank. 260/280 and 260/230 should be near 2.0–2.2. If you did not use on-column DNase: add 1/10 volume DNase buffer and 1 µL DNase Turbo, 30 min at 37 °C; add 1 µL more DNase Turbo (no extra buffer), another 30 min; add 1/10 volume DNase inactivation reagent, 5 min at room temperature with occasional flicking. Control PCR: use a few µL of each RNA as template for a normal PCR with primers you have used before (small product), plus a positive control with plasmid or genomic DNA. No product means no contaminating DNA. If there is product, repeat the DNase treatment. Do not skip this control. Re-measure concentration (it commonly drops after DNase). Optionally run ~8 µL on an RNA gel. One-step RT-qPCR (20 µL reaction) Component Volume One-step SYBR green master mix 10 µL Forward primer (5 µM) 1 µL Reverse primer (5 µM) 1 µL Nuclease-free water 4.5 µL One-step RT enzyme 0.5 µL RNA 3 µL For 8 reactions make a master mix of 80 µL master mix, 8 µL of each primer, 36 µL water, 4 µL RT enzyme; aliquot 17 µL per well and add 3 µL RNA last. Keep the plate and samples on ice. Cycling conditions were not recorded in the source; use the master-mix manufacturer’s settings.

Purpose Estimate the number of viable cells (colony-forming units, CFU) per mL of a culture by diluting it until individual colonies can be counted on plates. Materials Culture to be counted Sterile diluent: PBS or 7H9 for mycobacteria, PBS or saline for E. coli / S. aureus. Add 0.05% Tween 80 for mycobacteria to limit clumping. Sterile 1.5 mL tubes (or a 96-well plate for multichannel work) Agar plates (7H10/7H11 + supplements for mycobacteria; LB or TSA for E. coli / S. aureus) Fresh pipette tips for every transfer Procedure: tenfold dilutions Label one tube per dilution (10⁻¹ to 10⁻⁷, or as needed) and add 900 µL diluent to each. Mix the culture well (vortex, and for mycobacteria pipette up and down to break clumps). Transfer 100 µL of culture into the first tube (1:10, 10⁻¹). Mix thoroughly. With a fresh tip, transfer 100 µL from the 10⁻¹ tube into the next tube (10⁻²). Mix. Continue down the series with a fresh tip each time. Plate each dilution you need (see below). Include a no-culture diluent control. Incubate and count (see table). Shortcut dilutions: 1:9 means 1 part sample + 9 parts diluent (a tenfold dilution). 1:99 means 1 part + 99 parts (a 100-fold dilution), e.g. 10 µL + 990 µL. Plating Spread plating: spread 100 µL of a dilution over the plate. Count plates with 30–300 colonies. Drop plating (saves plates): spot 10 µL per dilution in a row on a plate (3 spots per dilution is typical). Let the drops dry before inverting. Count the spots with roughly 3–30 colonies. Counting and calculation $$\text{CFU/mL} = \frac{\text{colonies counted}}{\text{volume plated (mL)} \times \text{dilution}}$$ Example: 42 colonies from 100 µL (0.1 mL) of the 10⁻⁵ dilution: 42 / (0.1 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.2 × 10⁷ CFU/mL. Where several dilutions give countable plates, calculate each and report the mean. Incubation by organism E. coli S. aureus M. smegmatis BCG / M. tuberculosis Temperature 37 °C 37 °C 37 °C 37 °C Time to countable colonies overnight overnight (16–24 h) 3–4 days 3–4 weeks Plate medium LB TSA / LB 7H10/7H11 or LB 7H10/7H11 + OADC Seal mycobacterial plates in a bag so they do not dry out over long incubations. Work with BSL-2 organisms in a biosafety cabinet. Tips Always use a fresh tip between dilutions; carry-over inflates the counts at the high dilutions. Mix each tube before transferring. Settling or clumping is the biggest source of variation, especially in mycobacteria. Plate in duplicate or triplicate. For time-course killing assays, take the zero time point before adding drug and plate it at a dilution that can still be counted. If plates have no colonies at the lowest dilution you plated, report the result as below the limit of detection (one colony ÷ volume plated), not as zero. Check against your lab’s preferred diluent and drop-plating volume.

Wear gloves (contamination, and the chemicals are hazardous). Handle the gel gently; pressure creates artifacts. Use about 5 gel volumes of each solution. Make the sensitizing, silver nitrate and developing solutions fresh; fixing and quenching solutions can be made ahead. Fix in fixing solution at least 2 h or overnight, room temperature, gentle shaking. Ethanol washes: 30% ethanol, 20 min, gentle shaking; repeat once (removes detergents and salts). Sensitize: fresh sensitizing solution for only 2 min. Wash 3 × 30 s with water. Stain: silver nitrate staining solution (about 100 mg silver nitrate works well), 20 min, gentle shaking. Wash 3 × 15 s with deionized water. Do not wash longer or more times; too much washing removes the silver and gives artifacts. Develop: developing solution at room temperature, watching closely. Most gels take 2–7 min; up to 15 min for low protein amounts. Stop as soon as the desired contrast is reached and discard the solution immediately. Long development gives high background. In our hands ~0.02 µg protein was visible in the first 1–2 min. Quench: 50 mL 1% acetic acid for a few minutes. A quick rinse with water is enough for an image; extra water washes were not found to help. Solution recipes (reference set) The original protocol points to Green and Sambrook for its recipes. The Green and Sambrook recipes were not available to me, so the set below is the published Chevallet, Luche and Rabilloud (2006) formaldehyde/thiosulfate silver nitrate protocol, whose steps are close to the ones above. Check these against the recipes your lab used; step times above differ slightly (for example, 2 min sensitizing here vs 1 min in the published protocol). Solution Recipe Fixative 30% ethanol, 10% acetic acid Wash 20% ethanol, then water Sensitizer 0.8 mM sodium thiosulfate (0.02% w/v if using the pentahydrate) Silver nitrate 12 mM silver nitrate (stock typically 20% w/v, stored in the dark) Developer (make fresh) 3% potassium carbonate, 250 µL formalin per liter, 125 µL of 10% sodium thiosulfate per liter; add formalin ≤1 h before use Stop 4% (w/v) Tris, 2% (v/v) acetic acid (40 g Tris + 20 mL acetic acid per liter); the protocol above quenches in 1% acetic acid instead In the published version: fix ≥30 min; wash 2 × 10 min in 20% ethanol, 2 × 10 min in water; sensitize 1 min; rinse 2 × 1 min in water; silver 20 min–2 h; dip 10 s in water; develop (strongest bands appear in minutes, no progress after ~45 min); stop ≥30 min. For mass spectrometry downstream, a single 30 min fix gives the best sequence coverage, and aldehyde-free silver-ammonia variants, plus a ferricyanide–thiosulfate destain of excised bands, are described in the same paper. Reference: Chevallet M, Luche S, Rabilloud T. Silver staining of proteins in polyacrylamide gels. Nat Protoc 2006;1:1852–1858. Free preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/0706.4396

Fast, but yield is lower and DNA more sheared than in longer protocols. Enough for 50–100 PCRs and some downstream uses (e.g. transposon mapping of isolated clones). See also Nucleic acid extraction from M. smegmatis. Handle phenol and chloroform in a fume hood and dispose of them as hazardous waste. Pellet 10 mL of log-phase (OD 0.3 to 0.8) overnight culture. Resuspend in 400 µL 10 mM Tris pH 9 and transfer to a bead-beating tube with glass beads. Add 800 µL phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1, pH 8.0). Bead-beat 2 × 45 s. Spin 14,000 × g, 5 min. Transfer the upper aqueous layer (~150–300 µL; should be colorless) to a new tube. Add 1 µL 1 mg/mL RNase A; 37 °C for 30 min. (RNA co-precipitates and interferes with A260/280 quantification; skip if this does not matter.) Add 0.1 volume 3 M sodium acetate (pH 5.2), mix. Add 1 mL ice-cold ethanol, mix, and keep at –20 °C until you spin. Pellet 5–10 min at 14,000 × g in the cold. Remove ethanol. Wash the pellet with 1 mL ice-cold 70% ethanol, spin 5 min at room temperature, aspirate. Wash 4–5 more times with 70% ethanol (no spin). Spin 30 s to remove residual ethanol; dry 30 s to a few minutes. Resuspend in 50 µL water. NanoDrop. Typical yield ~1 µg/µL with A260/A280 ~2.0. Dilute to 20-50 ng/µL and use 1 µL per PCR. Qubit is preferable for quantification.

This protocol is different from the one on the recombineering page, including the inducer, induction timing and cell handling. The two have not been reconciled. Strains and plasmids M. smegmatis mc² wild type, with pJV53 (kanamycin; acetamide-inducible) or pNIT-recET-sacB (kanamycin). M. smegmatis ΔrecBCD (unmarked) on 7H10. ΔrecBCD carrying pJV53 (kanamycin) on 7H10 + kanamycin 25 µg/mL. ΔrecBCD carrying pNIT-recET-sacB-Zeo on 7H10 + zeocin 25 µg/mL. ΔrecBCD carrying pNIT-recET-sacB-Gent on 7H10 + gentamicin 10 µg/mL. This protocol is written for hygromycin-marked recombineering constructs. Protocol Keep kanamycin 25 µg/mL in the culture only until the preparation of competent cells. Add the inducer between OD 0.65 and 0.8 and incubate with shaking for 3 hours: caprolactam for pNIT, acetamide for pJV53. Final inducer concentration is 0.2%. Spin down and wash the culture with 10% glycerol 2–3 times (about 30–40 mL 10% glycerol for cells from a 25 mL culture). Resuspend the pellet in about one-tenth the volume of 10% glycerol (a little more concentrated is fine). More concentrated cells (from 50 mL into 1–2 mL) work as long as there is no arcing. Test the cells first with a no-DNA transformation: the time constant should be above 20 ms; below 15 ms the cells will most likely arc when DNA is added. Electroporate DNA into 400 µL of competent cells. After electroporation, transfer the cells to 4 mL 7H9 with no antibiotic (1 mL also works). Incubate with shaking at 37 °C for 3 hours. Spin down the cells and plate on two 7H10 + hygromycin 50 µg/mL plates (no kanamycin at any stage after making competent cells). More concentrated competent cells may need more than two hygromycin plates to avoid background hygromycin-resistant colonies. Pick 10–20 hygromycin-resistant colonies and restreak on 7H10 + hygromycin 50 µg/mL as small patches, enough for colony PCR and inoculation. After 2–3 days of growth, screen the clones by colony PCR. Grow 2–4 colony-PCR-positive clones in 7H9 + hygromycin 50 µg/mL for 2–3 days. Confirm again by PCR (2 µL of settled bacterial suspension in a 50 µL reaction). Streak out each culture on 7H10 + 15% sucrose plates to get isolated colonies. Colonies may stay tiny for a while. Dilute the cultures and plate undiluted, 10⁻² and 10⁻⁴ to get well-isolated colonies. A clone may occasionally become spontaneously kanamycin resistant, so plate 3–4 independent clones. Pick about 15–20 colonies per clone and streak first on kanamycin and then, with the same tip held in the same position, on hygromycin. This is critical; do not pick different inocula for the two plates. No more than 20 colonies per clone are needed. If no kanamycin-sensitive colonies appear in the first 15–20, discard that clone if others are available. Usually all, or more than 90%, of the colonies have lost the recET plasmid and are kanamycin sensitive; typically a kanamycin-sensitive colony appears within the first 6. Pick the clone from the corresponding hygromycin plate, grow in 7H9 + hygromycin, and make frozen stocks. Notes from the source First try the ΔrecBCD strain carrying pJV53. It works well in the author’s hands and the plasmid is not hard to lose. If making cell-wall mutants in the ΔrecBCD strain, compare your mutant phenotype with the parental unmarked ΔrecBCD and with wild-type mc²155 to confirm that the recBCD mutation itself does not contribute. No difference in polar growth or division was found.

Use this when day-to-day or other variance is a problem in assays such as kill curves, growth curves or screens. Grow the strain to log phase. Sonicate or filter the culture to make single-cell suspensions. This is not always necessary for M. smegmatis but is necessary for M. tuberculosis. Measure the OD of the sonicated or filtered culture. Dilute and make aliquots (200 µL to 1 mL per cryovial is fine) at an OD set by your desired starter-culture OD. For example, to start a 10 mL starter at OD 0.1, make 1 mL aliquots at OD 1. Freeze the aliquots. Some cells are lost on freeze–thaw, but the loss should be the same for each tube if you thaw them the same way each time. Subculture from an aliquot and run the assay when the culture reaches the OD you want. Sonicate before plating or seeding M. tuberculosis.

Naming strains Write the background strain first, then the modifications in the order they would appear in the genotype. Symbol Meaning geneK122P A point mutation: gene name, then the amino-acid change (lysine 122 to proline). Δ A deletion. :: An insertion into the chromosome, written site::insert. / An episomal vector; name the vector after the slash. For a non-coding mutation, give it a mutant number and list that number after the strain name, then describe the mutation elsewhere (for example in your strain database). Examples Deletion by recombineering: mc²155 ΔphoP::zeoR means phoP is deleted and a zeocin-resistance cassette sits at the locus. If the cassette is later removed by Cre: mc²155 ΔphoP::loxP. A tag added by recombineering: H37Rv phoP::FLAG-zeoR. An integrating vector: H37Rv L5::pKK216-phoP-FLAG means that vector is integrated at the L5 site. Vectors can be named for the person who made them or by a descriptive code. pKK216 was made by Karen Kieser and here was modified to add a C-terminal FLAG tag to phoP. An episomal vector: mc²155 / pUV15tetOR-phoP. The name carries information: a UV15 promoter plus tet operator and repressor. A strain with several modifications lists them in order, for example: mc²155 phoPK133P ΔphoR::hygR L5::pKK216-FLAG-phoR / pUV15tetOR-MSMEG_3717. Freezing down a strain Record the properly annotated strain in your lab strain list. In a 2 mL cryovial, mix 1 mL culture with 1 mL 50% glycerol. Store at −80 °C and record the box and position.

Follow your institution’s biosafety rules for every organism below, and work with BSL-2 mycobacteria (BCG and auxotrophic M. tuberculosis) in a biosafety cabinet. E. coli strains Strain Use Notes XL1-Blue General cloning Tetracycline resistant. Carries the tet repressor, which can help when cloning toxic genes under a tet-inducible promoter. Usually used as homemade chemical competent cells. DH5α General cloning No antibiotic resistance. Some constructs (for example, certain genes in pTetO vectors) are toxic here; XL1-Blue works better for those. Mach1 General cloning No antibiotic resistance. Grows faster than typical E. coli: transformations plated mid-morning give small colonies by evening, and colonies picked in the morning can be miniprepped by mid-afternoon. TOP10 General cloning Streptomycin resistant. Can be good for toxic genes. BL21 (DE3) Recombinant protein expression Chloramphenicol resistant. The pLysS form is selected with chloramphenicol 20 µg/mL. The Codon Plus form has extra rare tRNAs (useful for non-E. coli proteins) and is selected with chloramphenicol 40 µg/mL. Used for GST- and MBP-tagged proteins. BW25142 Replicating oriR6K plasmids DH5α background carrying pir. Supports more oriR6K plasmids than a pir DH5α strain. M. smegmatis mc²155 Selected for high transformation efficiency; carries a large chromosomal duplication. Grown in 7H9 + ADC; plated on LB or 7H10 + ADC. Wild type without antibiotic doubles about every 2.5 hours. M. bovis BCG Attenuated vaccine strain (BSL-2); lacks the ESX-1 locus among other changes. Grown in inkwells or roller bottles with tightly closed caps. 7H9 + ADC; plated on 7H10 + ADC. Doubles about every 18–20 hours. M. tuberculosis strains Use 7H9 with OADC (not ADC) for broth and plates. Leucine/pantothenate auxotroph: deletion of both leucine and pantothenate synthesis genes; virulence loci likely intact (BSL-2, biosafety cabinet); hygromycin resistant; doubles about every 24 hours. Grow in 7H9 + OADC with 50 µg/mL leucine and 24 µg/mL pantothenic acid. Grown in inkwells or roller bottles with tight caps. H37Rv: the standard virulent laboratory strain; doubles about every 24 hours; handled only in a BSL-3 facility; prone to PDIM loss and attenuation in mouse infection. Other strains seen in the literature include Erdman, CDC1551 and Beijing strains.

Use a tagged strain and an untagged control strain processed in parallel. Formaldehyde and PFA are toxic; work in a hood. Cross-link and lyse Grow 500 mL of each strain to OD₆₀₀ ~0.8. Pellet and resuspend in 100 mL PBS-Tween 80 + 800 µL 16% PFA. Keep on ice. (The first exposure and wash is to scavenge amine groups.) Pellet and resuspend again in 100 mL PBS-Tween 80 + 800 µL 16% PFA; incubate 1 h at 37 °C. Pellet and resuspend in 30 mL Buffer W (100 mM Tris pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA) + 0.1% DDM + protease inhibitor tablets. Lyse with a French press, 2× at up to 1,400 psi. Spin in Oakridge tubes at 15,000 × g for 15 min. Beads For each sample vortex the bead stock, move 600 µL to a tube, collect on a magnet, remove the supernatant, wash with 1 mL Buffer W, and resuspend in 400 µL Buffer W. Capture Pour the supernatant into 50 mL conicals. Save 200 µL as lysate. Dissolve the pellet in 30 mL denaturing wash buffer (8 M urea) to recover protein still in the membrane. Save 200 µL as pellet. Add 400 µL beads per sample (optimize for your protein and lysate). Rock for 2 h in the cold room. Spin 5,000 rpm, 5 min. Save 200 µL of supernatant as flow-through. Move the beads to microcentrifuge tubes. Wash 3× with Buffer W (magnet); save 100 µL of the first wash as wash. Elute and precipitate Add 160 µL PBS + 40 µL 5× Buffer BX. Vortex; incubate 10 min at room temperature; collect on the magnet and move the eluate to a new tube. Repeat once and combine. Add 100 µL 100% TCA to the eluate; keep in the fridge overnight. Add 25 µL 1× Laemmli to the beads (“beads” sample) and keep overnight. Spin the precipitate 15 min at 15,000 × g in the cold. Remove the supernatant. Wash with 1 mL acetone for 30–60 min in the fridge. Spin again 15 min. Remove the acetone (leave a little to protect the pellet), short spin, remove the rest, and air-dry 20–30 min. Resuspend in 25 µL 1× Laemmli. Add NaOH a microliter at a time until the dye is solid blue (orange or brown means too acidic). To reverse the cross-links, heat the sample at temperature and time per your protocol. Gels and mass spectrometry Analytical gel first: 5–10 µL of lysate, pellet, flow-through and wash per strain, plus ~0.5 µL concentrated eluate diluted into 10–15 µL buffer. If the pulldown worked, continue. Preparative gel: run the remaining eluates for the tagged and control strains, stain with Coomassie and look for bands unique to the tagged strain. Cut out the whole region around your protein for each sample and send for mass spectrometry. Keep only proteins more abundant in the pulldown than in the control in multiple independent pulldowns. See also MagStrep XT purification for the manufacturer’s bead protocol.

Cell lysate Inoculate 5 mL of seed culture into each of three 2 L flasks with 500 mL 7H9 (glycerol, supplement, 0.05% Tween 80) and grow at 30 °C for ~16–18 h. At mid-log (OD₆₀₀ 0.5–1.0), centrifuge at 8,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C in large bottles. Resuspend each pellet in 50 mM HEPES/NaOH pH 7.4 and move to a pre-weighed 50 mL conical. Spin 4,000 rpm, 10 min, 4 °C. Resuspend in 40 mL HEPES buffer; spin again; weigh the pellet. Resuspend at 1 g per 5 mL lysis buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 20% sucrose, 2 mM EGTA; recipe below) with 1/25 volume protease inhibitor cocktail (EDTA-free). Nitrogen cavitation: 1,850 psi (up to 2,200 psi) for 30 min with gentle swirling every 10 min. Release the pressure and collect. Repeat three times. Spin 4,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. Move the supernatant to a new tube (avoid the top “marshmallow” layer) and spin again. Gradient While cavitating, pour a 20–50% (w/v) linear sucrose gradient (gradient maker; long program), with 25 mM HEPES pH 7.4 in each solution. Layer 1.2 mL cleared lysate on top (200 µL × 6). Keep the rest as unfractionated (UF) material. Centrifuge in an SW40 swing-bucket rotor at 35,000 rpm (~218,000 × g) for 6 h at 4 °C. Collect fractions with a gradient fractionator (about 14 fractions, 0.5 speed, 6.67 mm per fraction) on an ice-water chamber. Wash the system with 50% ethanol then water afterwards. Aliquot 450 µL of each fraction into two tubes, snap-freeze in liquid nitrogen, and store at –80 °C. Keep ~100 µL for analysis. Practical details (step-by-step version) These come from the more detailed 2020 step-by-step and fill in handling steps the short version omits. Instrument specifics (BioComp Gradient Master and fractionator, SW40 rotor) are named as in the source; adapt to your equipment. Before the run - Start cooling the ultracentrifuge and rotor early (>1 h), with all buckets (and their gaskets) on the rotor, at 4 °C under vacuum. Run the pre-cool during the second cavitation. - Inspect the buckets: clean and dry, with the black gaskets in place; screw caps on unused buckets. Pouring the gradient (gradient maker) - Level the plate. Use ~6.5 mL of 20% sucrose and ~6.5 mL of 50% sucrose, both in 25 mM HEPES pH 7.4. Load the 20% first, then the 50% underneath; no bubbles anywhere in the syringe or tip (a bubble while applying the 50% will ruin the 20% layer). Fill above the centerline mark with your eye at the same height. - Do not wash the syringe or needle between uses (water dilutes the sucrose); wipe the outside of the needle before drawing a second 50% sucrose. - Cap the tube at an angle so all air escapes, remove excess sucrose from the cap, and run the 20–50% w/v program for your rotor (long program, SW40). Place finished gradients on ice in a pre-made hole. Loading and balancing - Position the tube on ice with the top of the gradient visible. Load 1.2 mL lysate as 200 µL aliquots, very slowly at first (the first aliquot is the hardest) so the gradient is not disturbed. - Balance on a balance in tube holders to within 10 mg; add lysate (or sucrose-buffer to a balance tube) to the lighter tube. Carry the uncovered ice bucket slowly. Wipe the tube exteriors, place in buckets, and hang all buckets (including empty ones) on the rotor. Collecting fractions - After the run, confirm the rotor has stopped, remove the tube gently with tweezers, check buckets for leaks, and carry the tube on ice to the fractionator. - Fractionator settings used: speed 0.5, distance 6.67 mm, 14 fractions in single mode; lower the suction cap to just before the first drop (fill the line with gradient solution; leftover water may come out first). The last fraction is ~0.5 mL; push the remaining gradient with air. Analysis Read the refractive index of 20 µL of each fraction to confirm the sucrose gradient. Mix 12 µL of each fraction with 4 µL 4× loading buffer, heat 95 °C for 5 min, and run all fractions on one gel (25 mA per gel) with a pre-stained standard. Transfer to PVDF in methanol-containing transfer buffer (110 V, 1 h, or 14 V overnight). Stain with Ponceau S, image, destain. Block 1 h in 5% milk in PBS + 0.05% Tween 20. Primary (example: anti-HA, 1:2,000), 1 h. Wash 3 × 10 min. HRP secondary (1:2,000), 1 h. Wash 3 × 10 min. Develop with ECL. Solutions 1 M HEPES pH 7.4: 23.8 g in ~80 mL water, adjust pH, make to 100 mL; store at –20 °C. 50% sucrose in 25 mM HEPES: 50 g sucrose + 2.5 mL 1 M HEPES + water to 100 mL; store at –20 °C. 20% sucrose in 25 mM HEPES: 20 g sucrose + 2.5 mL 1 M HEPES + water to 100 mL; store at –20 °C. 100 mM EGTA: 3.80 g in ~80 mL water; adjust to pH 8.0 to dissolve; make to 100 mL; store at 4 °C. Lysis buffer (45 mL): 675 µL 1 M HEPES, 18 mL 50% sucrose, 900 µL 100 mM EGTA, 25.43 mL water.

Reagent: SYTO 24 green fluorescent nucleic acid stain (Thermo Fisher, catalog S7559). The stock is a liquid. Dilute 1:10 in DMSO and aliquot (2 µL and 5 µL) into PCR tubes. Store in a foil-covered box at –20 °C in a desiccator. Stain with other dyes first (e.g. HADA) and complete their washes. Add 1 µL diluted SYTO 24 to 100 µL culture. Mount and image. No wash is needed. The dye is very bright. Reduce exposure settings so images are not saturated (see Image management).

Stock: 100% (w/v) trichloroacetic acid: dissolve 500 g TCA (as shipped) in 350 mL dH₂O; store at room temperature (see Sambrook & Russell, Molecular Cloning, for details on TCA precipitation). Add 1 volume TCA stock to 4 volumes of sample (e.g., 250 µL to 1.0 mL in a 1.5 mL tube; final ~20% TCA). Incubate 10 min at 4 °C. Spin 14,000 rpm, 5 min (microcentrifuge). Remove the supernatant without disturbing the pellet (whitish, fluffy). Wash with 200 µL cold acetone; spin 5 min. Repeat the wash once more (two acetone washes total). Dry the pellet by placing the open tube in a 95 °C heat block for 5–10 min to drive off the acetone. For SDS-PAGE add 2× or 4× sample buffer (± β-mercaptoethanol) and boil 10 min at 95 °C. Residual acid: if the sample buffer turns brown/yellow instead of blue, it is still acidic and will not dissolve or run well. Add 1 µL of saturated NaOH, pipette to mix, and repeat until it turns blue. The original says “saturated NaOH”; many labs use 1 M NaOH or Tris base instead. Confirm the concentration.

Purpose Identify induction conditions that produce a soluble protein of interest. Vary one variable at a time: temperature, induction time, IPTG concentration, lysis buffer, or medium. Procedure Inoculate 10 mL LB (+ antibiotic, e.g. ampicillin 140 µg/mL) with the transformant (expression strain such as BL21). Grow overnight. Next morning, take the OD₆₀₀. Inoculate 220 mL LB + antibiotic in a 250 mL flask to a starting OD of 0.1–0.25. Shake at 37 °C. Check the OD every 30–45 min and stop at OD₆₀₀ ~1–1.2. Pre-induction sample. Standardize to OD 5: $$\text{culture to take} = \frac{\text{desired OD}}{\text{current OD}} \times \text{final volume}$$ Example: culture at OD 1.0, final volume 100 µL: (5 / 1.0) × 100 µL = 500 µL. Spin 16,000 × g for 1 min, discard supernatant, resuspend in 100 µL 1× PBS, add 20 µL warmed 6× Laemmli, mix. Label “pre-induction”. 5. Split into four flasks of ~50 mL. 6. Induce with IPTG (usually 0.3–1.5 mM; 1 mM is the default; stock typically 500 mM). Volume = (final mM ÷ stock mM) × culture volume. Example: 0.8 mM in 55 mL = (0.8/500) × 55 mL = 88 µL. 7. Incubate at different temperatures (e.g. 20, 25, 37 °C) for 4 h. Lower temperatures usually give less protein but more of it soluble, and need longer induction. Some strains (e.g. cold-adapted chaperone strains) are only for very low temperatures. 8. Dilute each culture 1:9 (100 µL + 900 µL LB) to read OD accurately (the spectrophotometer is not linear above ~1), multiply by 10. 9. Make a normalized post-induction sample for each condition as in step 4 (e.g. OD 4.2: (5/4.2) × 100 = 119 µL). Label tubes with the condition before adding anything. 10. Spin the remaining culture 20 min at 4 °C (4,000 rpm); discard supernatant; freeze the pellet at –20 °C. Lysis Resuspend each pellet in 25–30 mL buffer without imidazole, plus 1 mM DTT (example: 50 mM Tris pH 7.9, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol). Most proteins are more soluble near neutral pH and ~150 mM NaCl; glycerol can help but may affect downstream assays. Lyse on ice (high-pressure homogenizer, French press or sonication; see your institution’s equipment training). Cool the centrifuge to 4 °C beforehand. Spin the lysate to separate soluble (supernatant) from insoluble (pellet) fractions. Supernatant and pellet samples Supernatant: normalize by the OD of the culture that the lysate came from (adjust for the volume of buffer used) so that equal cell equivalents are loaded. Example: OD 4.2 culture in 25 mL → (5/4.2) × 100 µL = 119 µL supernatant (concentrate by spinning, or use directly), made up to 100 µL with water, plus 20 µL 6× Laemmli. Pellet: resuspend in 5 mL 5 M urea to unfold the protein (pipette, vortex, or warm at 56 °C), then bring to the same volume as the supernatant with water or PBS. Make 100 µL samples the same way. For real purifications the soluble protein is in the supernatant and the pellet is only a diagnostic. Gel Load pre-induction, then post-induction, supernatant and pellet lanes for each condition (about 10–12 µL each; ~5 µL ladder). Run a Tris-tricine SDS-PAGE gel at constant current, 30 mA for the first 15 min, then ~38 mA until the dye reaches the bottom. Stain with Coomassie (30 s in a microwave inside a closed box, then 30 min gentle shaking; or 3 h to overnight at room temperature), destain, and photograph. Compare the band at the expected size between supernatant and pellet at each condition. Lysis by French press (variant) A second, narrative version of this protocol used a French press for lysis: Resuspend cell pellets in ~25 mL of 50 mM Tris pH 7.9 (try different buffers; most proteins are soluble near neutral pH and ~150 mM NaCl) and keep on ice. Grease the gasket on the plunger, head piece and screw with vacuum grease. Put the plunger in the cell, invert it in the stand, pour in the suspension, leave the screw open so air can escape, fit the head piece while holding the plunger up, then close the screw fully. Turn the cell right-side up in the press, set the dial to high, and start the pump with a collection tube under the outlet. Watch the pressure; you want it to reach ~1000 before much suspension has flowed out. Units of “1000” not given in the source. When dripping stops, turn the pump off, switch to medium while still collecting, open the screw to drain the rest, then lower the plunger. Pass the cells through a second time if the pressure did not build or the suspension is not clear. Clean thoroughly: rinse so water runs through all holes in the head piece, then wipe and dry. Balance in Oakridge tubes (to within about a tenth of a gram, in pairs) and spin 20,000 rpm, 20 min, 4 °C. Convert to ×g for your rotor. Worked example for loading: if the lysate is concentrated 2× relative to the induction culture (resuspended in half the volume), double each OD to estimate its OD-equivalent, then adjust: a sample at OD-equivalent 4.2 needs 5/4.2 × 10 µL ≈ 12 µL instead of 10 µL on the gel (maximum ~15 µL per lane).

Part of the Tn-seq workflow. Start from a titered phage stock (phage stock preparation). Add Tween 80 to the selection plates: it inhibits the lytic cycle, so you avoid recovering mostly phage DNA. Include a no-phage control to measure kanamycin background. Aim for at least ~200,000 independent colonies per library; too-crowded plates lose signal from some mutants. Common core Grow cells to the OD in the table; wash with MP buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10 mM MgSO₄, 2 mM CaCl₂). Resuspend in warm (37 °C) MP buffer; warm the phage to 37 °C too (the Benchling version pre-warms wash and resuspension media and the centrifuge to 37 °C so the temperature-sensitive phage does not become lytic at the 30 °C permissive temperature). Mix cells and phage, incubate at 37 °C. Plate on kanamycin + Tween 80, incubate, scrape, freeze in aliquots with glycerol; titer one thawed aliquot. Versions A. Mtb-style (Murry/Rego edits) B. M. smegmatis-optimized C. Benchling (Fortune lab, 2022) Culture 100 mL, OD₆₀₀ 0.6–1.0, 7H9 + glycerol + OADC (ADC for smeg/BCG) + 0.05% Tween 50 mL (up to 200 mL for bigger libraries) at OD₆₀₀ 2–3; late log/stationary is critical 100 mL Mtb, OD 1.0–1.5, 7H9 + OADC + Tween Wash 2 × 10–25 mL MP 3 × MP 2 × 50 mL 7H9 + glycerol + OADC without Tween, pre-warmed to 37 °C Resuspend 10 mL warm MP ~5 mL MP to a 6 mL final volume after phage 5 mL medium without Tween Phage ~2×10¹¹ 2–3×10¹² (1×10¹¹ per OD unit); ~5 mL if stock is only ~10¹¹ PFU/mL ~2.5 mL high-titer phage Incubation 3–4 h (generic) or overnight (Mtb), 37 °C 4 h, 37 °C, shaking ~18 h, 37 °C, no shaking After Spin, resuspend, plate (or freeze and titer first) Plate at once Optional PBS + Tween wash, resuspend in 2 mL Plates 10 × 150 mm 7H10 + Tween + Kan 25 µg/mL, 250 µL each ~20 × 15 cm LB + Kan + 0.1% Tween 80, 600 µL each, glass beads; square plates also work 10 × 150 mm or 3 × 225 mm 7H10 + OADC + Tween + Kan 50 µg/mL Growth ~3 weeks, 37 °C 3 days, 37 °C ~21 days, agar side up, foil-wrapped Harvest scrape, prep gDNA scrape into 7H9 + 15% glycerol, pool, aliquot at −80 °C scrape into buffer or 7H9 + glycerol Yield target ~200,000 ≥200,000–300,000 dense, nearly a lawn Notes: - Kanamycin differs between sources (20, 25 and 50 µg/mL). The M. smegmatis source writes “20 ml/ml”; this is assumed to mean 20 µg/mL. - Phage titers above 5×10¹¹ PFU/mL are not always obtained; scale phage volume to the titer. - “Lacy” phage plates are hard to get; test a dilution series and then scale up the best dilution to 5–10 plates. - Mtb work is BSL3. Wrap and incubate plates for the full time. For scraping, freezing and DNA extraction, continue with library prep and sequencing.

Part of the Tn-seq workflow. Start from the frozen library from library construction. Overall design. Genomic DNA is fragmented, ends are repaired and A-tailed, and an annealed adapter carrying a random barcode is ligated. Adapter 1 carries a 3′ amine so it cannot be extended. PCR 1 amplifies from a transposon-specific primer to the adapter, so only transposon-containing fragments amplify. After size selection, PCR 2 adds Illumina flow-cell and index sequences. The random barcode lets you collapse PCR duplicates to unique templates during analysis. 1. Scrape and freeze the library Per sample: 5 mL 7H9 + OADC + Tween and 5 mL 50% glycerol in a 50 mL tube. Scrape each plate vertically then horizontally into the corner, pour into the tube, pool all plates of one sample, vortex, aliquot ~2 mL into ~6 cryovials, store at −80 °C, and titer one aliquot after thaw. (Scraping 30 plates takes 8–9 h; 36 plates took 2.5–3 h in one report.) 2. Genomic DNA (bead beating and phenol–chloroform) Thaw 4 mL library (2 vials), spin at 5,000 × g, 10 min; resuspend in 2 mL TE pH 8.0. Add 750 µL to each of 3 bead-beating tubes containing 600 µL phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1, pH 8.0). Bead beat at max speed 45 s, rest on ice 45 s (let the instrument cool 1 min between samples); 4 rounds total. Spin 21,000 × g, 10 min; move the aqueous layer to a 15 mL tube with 1 volume of phenol:chloroform. Rock 1 h at room temperature (all in a fume hood, double-bagged). Transfer to a phase-lock tube, spin 1,500 × g, 5 min, 4 °C. Add ½ volume chloroform, spin again. Move the aqueous phase to a new phase-lock tube. Add RNase A to 25 µg/mL, 1 h at 37 °C with shaking. Repeat the phenol:chloroform then chloroform extraction. Add 1/10 volume 3 M sodium acetate pH 5.2 and 1 volume isopropanol; invert; precipitate at −20 °C overnight. Spin ~5,000 × g, 10 min, 4 °C; wash 3 × with 5 mL 70% ethanol; dry ~5 min (do not over-dry); resuspend in 500 µL–1 mL nuclease-free water (warm to 37–56 °C if needed). Quantify by Qubit BR. 3. Fragment the DNA (choose one) Goal: fragments of 200–500 bp, peak ~300 bp. Check ~5 µL on a 2% TBE gel; a smear from ~100 bp to ~1 kb with a peak at 300–400 bp is expected. Elute in water (warm to 50–65 °C) after clean-up. Option Input Settings Notes Acoustic, Covaris v8 (2015) 5 µg in 130 µL TE in Covaris tube (part 520045), pipette through the slit in the lid duty 10%, intensity 5, 200 cycles/burst, 180 s Cool the instrument first (~2 h). Clean up with a spin column (Qiagen), elute 50 µL. Acoustic, other instrument/model (MRS version) 5 µg in 130 µL 140 W peak incident power, duty 10%, 200 cycles/burst, 80 s; or duty 10%, intensity 4, 200 cycles/burst, 80 s Settings depend on the instrument; calibrate. Acoustic, Benchling as above 5%, intensity 3, 200 cycles/burst, 110 s Covaris calibration can drift; always check size on a gel. Enzymatic, NEBNext Ultra II FS 500 ng gDNA (up to 2 µg if you need 1 µg downstream) in 26 µL 1× TE 26 µL DNA + 7 µL reaction buffer + 2 µL enzyme mix; 37 °C for 15–30 min (20 min typical), 65 °C 30 min, 4 °C hold; heated lid 75 °C Time sets size: 30 min gave a peak near 150 bp in one trial, so try 15–20 min. Clean up with a spin column (3 × 30 s PE washes, elute 50 µL water at 65 °C). Spin-column notes (shared by all versions): a Qiagen PCR column binds up to ~10–15 µg; do 3 × 30 s PE washes instead of one 1-min wash; elute in warm water or buffer, let it sit ~1 min. Kit reference: NEBNext Ultra II FS DNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB E7805) https://www.neb.com/en-us/products/e7805-nebnext-ultra-ii-fs-dna-library-prep-kit-for-illumina 4. Anneal adapters Adapter 1 (short, 3′-NH₂): 5′-TAC CAC GAC CA-NH₂-3′. Adapter 2 (barcoded): 5′-ATG ATG GCC GGT GGA TTT GTG NNA NNA NNN TGG TCG TGG TAT-3′. (The different sources name these 1.1/1.2 and 2.1/2.2/3.1; the sequences are the same.) 2 µL 2 mM MgCl₂ + 24 µL adapter 1 (100 µM) + 24 µL adapter 2 (100 µM). Anneal: 95 °C 4–5 min, then −1 °C/min to 20 °C, hold at 20 °C. Do not let annealed adapters warm up again (keep at 20 °C or on ice). Aliquot and freeze at −20 °C; thaw on ice and discard leftovers. Dilute to ~20 µM in 10 mM Tris + 10 mM NaCl before ligation if your ligase module requires 15–25 µM (e.g., 20 µL adapters + 30 µL buffer). One version lists adapter stocks as 1 mM rather than 100 µM; the 100 µM figure is used in the two later versions. 5. End repair/A-tail and adapter ligation 1 µg fragmented DNA in 65 µL with 3 µL End Prep enzyme mix and 6.5 µL 10× buffer; 20 °C 30 min, 65 °C 30 min, hold 4 °C (NEBNext Ultra End Repair/dA-Tailing Module E7546). The Benchling version uses KAPA HyperPrep or NEB Ultra kits per insert (KAPA: 7 µL buffer + 3 µL enzyme, 50 µL total). Add to the same tube: 30 µL NEBNext Ultra II Ligation Master Mix (E7595), 2.5 µL annealed adapter (diluted), 1 µL ligation enhancer. Incubate 20 °C, 30 min (heated lid off). Earlier version: 15 µL ligase mix, 60 min. Benchling/KAPA: 60 µL DNA + 4 µL adapter + 30 µL buffer + 10 µL ligase, 60 min at 20 °C. Clean up with AMPure XP at 1.8× (a lower ratio may work): add beads, mix 10×, 5 min, magnet ~3 min, two 70–80% ethanol washes (fresh), elute in ~40 µL water, transfer ~36 µL. Expect ~700–800 ng from 1 µg; quantifying here is not needed. Alternatively use a spin column. 6. PCR 1 (transposon junction amplification) Primers: transposon primer (anneals in the transposon) 5′-GTCTAGAGACCGGGGACTTATC-3′; adapter primer 5′-ATGATGGCCGGTGGATTTGTG-3′. v8 (2015) Revised enzymatic (2019–20) Benchling (2024) Polymerase KAPA HiFi HotStart + GC buffer KAPA HotStart ready mix + DMSO NEB Q5 master mix Template ~800 ng total (32.5 µL), 50 µL 4 × 50 µL reactions, ~90 ng each (<100 ng or Mg²⁺ is chelated) ½ of ligated DNA (~300–400 ng) in 50 µL Cycling 98 °C 5 min; 15 × (98 °C 60 s, 65 °C 30 s, 72 °C 30 s); 72 °C 10 min 98 °C 5 min; 15 × (98 °C 1 min, 65 °C 30 s, 72 °C 15 s); 72 °C 3 min 98 °C 5 min; 14 × (98 °C 60 s, 65 °C 30 s, 72 °C 30 s); 72 °C 10 min Clean-up Qiagen, elute 35 µL, normalize to 30 ng/µL pool, Qiagen (3 PE washes), elute 35 µL; Qubit; 30 ng/µL in 50 µL spin column or 1.8× AMPure, elute 32 µL Tris-Tween One later edit used 67 °C annealing in PCR 1; the others use 65 °C. Include a water-only control and check ~2 µL on a 2% gel (diffuse band, ~300–600 bp). 7. Size selection (to ~300–400 bp) Illumina paired-end reads work best near 300 bp; selection must be done after PCR 1 (or after PCR 2). Recovery is very low; 10 ng or more does not bottleneck the library. Method Notes E-gel SizeSelect II (2%) Load ≤700 ng per lane (hence the 30 ng/µL dilution); run ~15 min, then to the 350 bp collection point; recover 25 µL. PippinPrep (2% dye-free cassette) Mix with loading dye; select 300–400 bp range or 350 bp tight; ~1 h; ~1 ng/µL in ~40 µL. Preferred in one version. AMPure double selection Optimize the ratio (≈0.6–0.8× to remove large fragments, then bind the rest); higher throughput. Agarose gel (2%) Cut and gel-extract; higher cross-contamination risk. Quantify with Qubit HS if needed (or skip; low-yield results are normal). 8. PCR 2 (Illumina ends, index) Transposon-side primer (“Sol-Mar mix”): four versions with a 5–8 nt variable spacer to stagger the first bases and avoid single-color clusters; mix 1:1:1:1. 5′-AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT-N(5–8)-CGGGGACTTATCAGCCAACC-3′ Adapter-side indexed primer (8-nt index XXXXXXXX; each sample gets a different index): 5′-CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGAT-XXXXXXXX-GTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGTGCTCTTCCGATCTATGATGGCCGGTGGATTTGTG-3′ The transposon primer ends 5 bp from the junction so reads begin with TGTTA, a specificity check in analysis. Typical reaction (50 µL): polymerase mix, 2.5 µL SolMar mix, 2.5 µL indexed primer, size-selected DNA (10–100 ng; one source used 300 ng), water. Use a touchdown program, e.g., 98 °C 5 min; 8 cycles of (98 °C 1 min, 68 °C → −0.8 °C/cycle, 68 °C 15 s); then 8 cycles of (98 °C 1 min, 62 °C 30 s, 68 °C 15 s); 68 °C 5 min. (v8: 16 cycles of the touchdown program; Benchling: Q5 with the PCR 1 program.) Clean up with AMPure (0.8–0.9×; elute 30 µL and take 26 µL). Run on a gel: a tight band at ~300–350 bp (a second band at about double that size has been seen; cause not established). Quantify by Qubit BR and qPCR (use qPCR molarity for loading). Yield >25 ng/µL is wanted (10 ng/µL workable); one report lost ~90% of the DNA in this step. Optional check of library diversity: blunt TOPO cloning of the library, M13 colony PCR of ~10 colonies, and sequencing (see blunt TOPO cloning). 9. Pool and submit for sequencing Pool equal volumes of each indexed library (≥10 µL total required by many cores; lo-bind tubes). Typical order: Illumina paired-end, medium kit, Read 1 = 78 cycles, index = 10, Read 2 = 78 cycles, 20% PhiX spike-in, at least ~130 million reads per lane; list the library as an amplicon/custom Tn-seq library, and request TapeStation and qPCR QC. Enter the reverse complement of the index sequence if the core asks for “Index Read 1” (the index is read in its own cycle with the Read 2 primer). The reason for 20% PhiX is not stated in the source; it is thought to offset the low-diversity and high-GC content. Library submission details are written for one sequencing core; check your own core’s form. 10. Analysis Decompress the facility’s fastq.bz2 files, check FastQC per lane, merge lanes per sample if consistent, then run TPP (maps reads with BWA, collapses barcodes to template counts, writes .wig files) and Transit. Do not use newer Python packages than Transit’s docs list. See https://transit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tpp.html and https://transit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/transit_install.html. Notes Always run a water-only control through the PCRs. Keep a record of which index went to which sample. Qubit and qPCR disagree on library concentration; use qPCR for flow-cell loading.

Tn-seq protocols for mycobacteria have been passed between labs and edited many times, so several versions of each step exist and they do not always agree. They are not different methods so much as different tunings of the same method. This page shows the order of steps, which page covers each, and where the versions differ. Pick one version per step and stay with it for a whole experiment. The method is the Himar1 mariner transposon (φMycoMarT7, a temperature-sensitive phage carrying the transposon and a kanamycin marker) delivered by phage transduction (Murry et al. 2008), followed by sequencing of transposon–genome junctions. Workflow Step What happens Page 1 Make a high-titer, temperature-sensitive phage stock Phage stock preparation 2 Transduce, plate on kanamycin, scrape, freeze the library Library construction by transduction 3 Extract genomic DNA, shear, add adapters, amplify junctions, size-select, add Illumina ends Library prep and sequencing 4 Map reads and count insertions at TA sites Analysis with TPP and Transit (see links below) (side) Find the insertion site of one individual mutant Manual insertion mapping Where the versions differ Step Version Key differences Phage stock Murry 2008 / Mtb-lab edits Wash host cells in 7H9 + glycerol + ADC without Tween; 10-cm 7H10 plates; titer by spotting. Phage stock M. smegmatis-optimized LB plates throughout; host washed in MP buffer; use within 3 days; fresh stock per transduction. Transduction Mtb-style (Murry/Rego) ~100 mL culture at OD 0.6–1.0; ~2×10¹¹ phage; 37 °C overnight; 7H10 + Tween + Kan; ~3 weeks. Transduction M. smegmatis-optimized 50–200 mL culture at OD 2–3; ~1×10¹¹ phage per OD unit; 4 h at 37 °C; LB + Kan + Tween; 3 days. Transduction Benchling (Fortune lab, 2022) BSL3 Mtb: OD 1.0–1.5; ~18 h unshaken at 37 °C; optional PBS-Tween wash; ~21 days. DNA shearing Acoustic (Covaris) Several parameter sets; see variant table on the library-prep page. DNA shearing Enzymatic (NEBNext Ultra II FS) 500 ng input; 15–30 min at 37 °C; no instrument needed. Junction PCR KAPA HiFi or HotStart vs Q5 Different polymerase, cycles and annealing temperature. Size selection E-gel, PippinPrep, AMPure beads, agarose gel Same goal (~300–400 bp); different tradeoffs.
